meta.description: Candidate backlog for quotle.info ingestion. Documented misattribution/famous-quote targets from Wikiquote + Quote Investigator, harvested by the harvest-candidates Workflow. Managed by tools/harvest.js — do not hand-edit counts. Lifecycle: queued → selected → ingested (or skipped).

candidates.quote: The more I practice, the luckier I get.
candidates.trueOrigin: The luck-and-hard-work family traces to Coleman Cox, 'Listen to This' (1922); golfer Gary Player popularized the golf phrasing
candidates.whyNotable: Golf's most-circulated 'luck' line predates every golfer it's credited to, going back to Coleman Cox in 1922.

candidates.quote: Many people think they are thinking when they are merely rearranging their prejudices
candidates.trueOrigin: Bishop William Fitzjames Oldham; earliest documented 1906 in Zion's Herald (also later credited to Edward R. Murrow and William James)
candidates.whyNotable: A widely circulated aphorism pinned on Rockne (who quoted it in a 1926 newspaper column, in quotation marks, without claiming it); QI reassigns the origin to Methodist bishop William Fitzjames Oldham, documented in 1906.

candidates.quote: An acre of performance is worth a whole world of promise
candidates.trueOrigin: James Howell, British historian, 1655 (in his published collection of familiar letters); later also misattributed to William Dean Howells via name confusion.
candidates.whyNotable: Several 2006 Auerbach remembrance pieces credited this line to him, but QI shows he only borrowed it; the phrase originated with British historian James Howell in 1655 ('An acre of performance is worth the whole Land of promise').

candidates.quote: Sometimes I sits and thinks, and sometimes I just sits.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI traces it to an anonymous Maine fisherman quoted in February 1905 (via the Boston Record); the Paige credit is a retroactive 2009 newspaper misattribution. Also misattributed to A. A. Milne and Lucy Maud Montgomery.
candidates.whyNotable: A folksy line frequently credited to Paige, but QI documents it circulating from a 1905 Maine fisherman decades before Paige was famous.

candidates.quote: Always go to other people's funerals; otherwise they won't go to yours.
candidates.trueOrigin: Appeared in Punch magazine, January 1911 or earlier
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared as a Berra witticism, but Wikiquote traces the joke to Punch magazine (1911 or earlier), long before it was ever pinned on Berra.

candidates.quote: Never answer an anonymous letter.
candidates.trueOrigin: A 19th-century joke predating Berra
candidates.whyNotable: A commonly repeated Yogi-ism, but Wikiquote dates the joke to the 19th century; Berra initially denied it before later embracing the attribution.

candidates.quote: Nobody goes there anymore. It's too crowded.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous joke in early-20th-century newspapers; assigned to Berra in 1962
candidates.whyNotable: A classic paradox routinely credited to Berra, but QI documents the gag in early-20th-century newspapers, with the attribution to Berra only appearing in 1962.

candidates.quote: Say anything you want. Just spell my name right.
candidates.trueOrigin: Long-running showbiz trope; QI's earliest strong evidence is P. T. Barnum (1888 newspapers), predating the Ruth attribution by decades.
candidates.whyNotable: A publicity catchphrase pinned on Ruth (a 1932 Florida column) that QI reassigns: the earliest strong evidence is P. T. Barnum in 1888, and the line is a widespread trope also credited to Cohan, Mae West and others.

candidates.quote: It's not the will to win but the will to prepare to win that makes the difference.
candidates.trueOrigin: Predates Bryant; QI traces versions to Fielding Yost (1930) and Vernon Law (1965)
candidates.whyNotable: Bryant is the popular attribution, but the formulation circulated in sports decades before him.

candidates.quote: There are three types of people: those who make things happen, those who watch things happen, and those who wonder what happened
candidates.trueOrigin: Nicholas Murray Butler, President of Columbia University, in a March 1931 speech at the University of California ('There are the few who make things happen, the many more who watch things happen, and the overwhelming majority who have no notion of what happens')
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-shared motivational maxim pinned on many names; QI traces it to Butler in 1931 and lists Casey Stengel among the people incorrectly credited.

candidates.quote: Failing to prepare is preparing to fail.
candidates.trueOrigin: A pre-existing proverb; Wooden only repeated an aphorism already circulating in the 1920s when he was a youth. Variants are also pinned on Benjamin Franklin.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared Wooden 'coach wisdom' lines, but Wikiquote's Misattributed section notes he merely repeated an aphorism decades older than his career.

candidates.quote: Sports do not build character. They reveal it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Sports commentator Heywood Hale Broun, who used the idea in speeches in 1974 ('sport doesn't build character... Sports reveals character'); James Michener's 1976 book likely polished it into the modern wording.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely-shared 'wise coach' line pinned on Wooden, but QI's earliest match (Ames Daily Tribune, Jan 1974) credits CBS sportscaster Heywood Hale Broun, not Wooden.

candidates.quote: Show me a good loser and I'll show you an idiot.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous; Quote Investigator's earliest exact match is Gus Doerner (1962), 'Show me a good loser and I'll show you a loser.' Durocher's own 1975 phrasing was 'Show me a good loser in professional sports, and I'll show you an idiot.' Also widely credited to Knute Rockne and others.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently pinned on Durocher (who used a version in his 1975 book), but Quote Investigator concludes the adage's creator is anonymous, with the earliest exact match traced to Gus Doerner in 1962 and semantic precursors circulating earlier.

candidates.quote: My way of joking is to tell the truth. That's the funniest joke in the world
candidates.trueOrigin: Said by promoter Don King to George Foreman (per Wikiquote Misattributed section)
candidates.whyNotable: Printed in Ali's own autobiography 'The Greatest,' but Wikiquote flags it as a line actually spoken by Don King to George Foreman.

candidates.quote: How old would you be if you didn't know how old you was?
candidates.trueOrigin: QI tentatively credits Rev. Clarence H. Wilson (1927 sermon); the saying was likely already circulating and was pinned on Paige only by the 1970s (Ruth Gordon/Garson Kanin, and 1977 U.S. House aging-committee testimony).
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared 'Satchel Paige' lines on the internet, but QI finds no early Paige source and traces the earliest match to a 1927 sermon.

candidates.quote: Show me a good loser and I'll show you a loser
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous / early-twentieth-century sports culture. QI found the earliest exact match in 1962 (coach Gus Doerner), with semantic precursors back to 1904 (e.g. Robert Zuppke's 1924 'A good loser is no good'); no solid evidence for Lombardi.
candidates.whyNotable: A hard-edged winning maxim routinely pinned on Lombardi; QI finds no support for him and traces the exact wording to Gus Doerner in 1962.

candidates.quote: The dictionary is the only place where success comes before work
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous. Earliest strong match is the Oklahoma City Star in 1934 ('The only place where SUCCESS comes before WORK is in the dictionary'), evolved from 1920s jokes; also misattributed to Mark Twain, Arthur Brisbane, and Vidal Sassoon.
candidates.whyNotable: A pun-quote credited to Lombardi (and Twain, and Sassoon); QI shows the anonymous 1934 newspaper origin predates every named attribution.

candidates.quote: The will to win is not worth much unless you have the will to prepare to win
candidates.trueOrigin: Fielding H. Yost, University of Michigan football coach, who expressed the idea in his 1929-30 Wingate Memorial Lectures; QI names Yost the leading candidate for creator. The Lombardi attribution appears to have spread after his 1970 death.
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly shared as Lombardi motivational wisdom (often as 'Everyone has the will to win but few have the will to prepare to win'); QI traces the concept to Yost decades earlier.

candidates.quote: Winning isn't everything; it's the only thing
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry 'Red' Sanders, UCLA football coach, in a 1948 speech to the Birmingham Quarterback Club (earliest documented instance, The Birmingham News, Nov 9 1948). Lombardi himself denied saying it; his real line was 'Winning isn't a sometime thing; it's an all the time thing.'
candidates.whyNotable: The single most famous fake-Lombardi quote of all time; both Wikiquote and QI reassign it to Red Sanders, who framed it as a joke about zealous fans.

candidates.quote: Success is never final, failure is never fatal. It is the courage to continue that counts.
candidates.trueOrigin: No solid Churchill source; QI finds it a floating aphorism. Wooden used a version as a 1972 chapter epigraph with a footnote crediting Churchill, which helped spread the false Churchill ascription.
candidates.whyNotable: Appears on QI's John Wooden tag because Wooden footnoted it to Churchill; the dominant popular credit is Churchill, for whom QI finds no real source.

candidates.quote: It's tough to make predictions, especially about the future.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mid-20th-century Danish proverb; not originated by Berra
candidates.whyNotable: Constantly attributed to Berra (and sometimes Niels Bohr), but Wikiquote flags it as a mid-20th-century proverb of Danish origin, not Berra's.

candidates.quote: If people don't want to come out to the ballpark, nobody's going to stop them
candidates.magnetAuthor: Yogi Berra (also credited to Casey Stengel via his Kansas City remark)
candidates.creditedTo: Yogi Berra (also credited to Casey Stengel via his Kansas City remark)
candidates.trueOrigin: Impresario Sol Hurok, per a 1952 gossip column ('If people don't want to come, nothing will stop them'); QI documents a parallel Stengel version about Kansas City attendance
candidates.whyNotable: A classic 'Yogiism' about attendance; QI traces the underlying saying to Sol Hurok in 1952 and documents a Stengel-attributed Kansas City variant.

candidates.quote: Skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been.
candidates.trueOrigin: Walter Gretzky (Wayne's father), who taught it to Wayne as a child
candidates.whyNotable: The business-seminar staple is almost always credited to Wayne, but the advice originated with his father Walter, as documented by Legends Revealed.

candidates.quote: In theory there is no difference between theory and practice; in practice there is.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest known source is Walter J. Savitch's 1984 book, quoting an anonymous conference remark
candidates.whyNotable: A favorite among engineers who credit Berra, but Wikiquote's earliest source is a 1984 computer-science book quoting it as an overheard conference remark, unconnected to Berra.

candidates.quote: The future ain't what it used to be.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paul Valéry (1937), rendered in English 1948; Laura Riding & Robert Graves used it in English in 1937
candidates.whyNotable: Widely pinned on Berra, but QI and Wikiquote trace the English phrasing to 1937 (Paul Valéry / Laura Riding & Robert Graves), decades before Berra was quoted.

candidates.quote: Find the good and praise it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Madison Babcock, Superintendent of Schools, San Francisco, in an 1896 annual report ('Find the good and praise it, speak sparingly of the bad')
candidates.whyNotable: Popularly credited to Alex Haley (who admitted seeing it on a bumper sticker) and entangled with Owens's own 'find the good' phrasing; QI reassigns the exact wording to schools superintendent Madison Babcock (1896).

candidates.quote: All wars are planned by older men in council rooms apart
candidates.trueOrigin: Grantland Rice, from his poem 'The Two Sides of War' (originally 'Two Sides of War'), published in his syndicated 'Sportlight' column in the New York Tribune, 1921. QI confirms Rice as the originator but documents that the line is widely misattributed to Herman Melville, Herbert Hoover, and a Reverend E. W. Elstron; earlier thematically-similar (but differently worded) verses by Timothy Parker (1864) and Melville (1866) fuel the confusion.
candidates.whyNotable: Genuinely Grantland Rice's 1921 anti-war poem line, but it is one of the internet's most-misattributed verses — routinely pinned on Herman Melville or Herbert Hoover; QI traces the exact wording back to Rice.

candidates.quote: You don't have to be crazy to work here, but it helps.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous comedic template ('You don't have to be X to Y but it helps') documented from June 1920, over a decade before it was attributed to Disney.
candidates.whyNotable: Credited to Disney via his secretary in a 1933 newspaper, but QI shows it is a 'snowclone' joke template with anonymous instances dating to 1920, so Disney did not originate it.

candidates.quote: The harder I practice, the luckier I get
candidates.trueOrigin: No single originator; a centuries-old family of proverbial 'work/practice = luck' maxims. Gary Player credited fellow golfer Jerry Barber (1962); a 'hard work' version dates to 1949 and knowledge-based variants to 1896.
candidates.whyNotable: One of golf's most-shared 'lucky' lines, pinned interchangeably on Arnold Palmer, Gary Player, Lee Trevino and others; QI shows it predates all of them and has no true author.

candidates.quote: in the zone
candidates.trueOrigin: Tennis-tour slang that Ashe popularized in his 1974 audio diary ('he is in what we call the zone'); QI says he may have participated in its coinage but did not solely originate it, and the term circulated among pros and is tied to the TV show 'The Twilight Zone.'
candidates.whyNotable: Ashe is widely credited with coining the sports phrase 'in the zone,' but Quote Investigator finds the term was already circulating among tennis pros when he documented it in 1974.

candidates.quote: Every strike brings me closer to the next home run.
candidates.trueOrigin: No contemporaneous source; earliest documented appearance is circa 2001, long after Ruth died in 1948.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely shared motivational line credited to Ruth, but the earliest sourcing Wikiquote can find dates only to 2001 — more than 50 years after Ruth's death — a classic apocryphal-attribution red flag.

candidates.quote: What the hell has Hoover got to do with it? Anyway, I had a better year than he did.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anecdote first recorded by sportswriter Tom Meany in 'Babe Ruth: The Big Moments of the Big Fellow' (1947), ~15 years after the alleged remark; no contemporaneous source.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-repeated Babe Ruth anecdotes (his 1932 salary holdout out-earning President Hoover); QI finds no contemporaneous 1930-33 source and traces the earliest telling to Tom Meany's 1947 biography, calling it probably-said but unverified.

candidates.quote: Yesterday's home runs don't win today's games.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unattributed folk saying circulating by 1959; retrofitted onto Ruth decades after his 1948 death.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared as Ruth wisdom, but Wikiquote flags it as unattributed folk wisdom appearing by 1959 with no link to Ruth until roughly the 1980s, nearly 30 years later.

candidates.quote: Cunningham did more for integration in Alabama in 60 minutes than Martin Luther King Jr. did in 20 years.
candidates.trueOrigin: An apocryphal locker-room line tied to Sam 'Bam' Cunningham's 1970 USC win over Alabama; the anecdote is widely retold but its authenticity and exact wording are contested, and Wikiquote files it only as 'attributed' (Christian Science Monitor, 2005).
candidates.whyNotable: A beloved but heavily contested civil-rights anecdote; Wikiquote lists it only under 'Attributed' and historians dispute whether Bryant ever said it.

candidates.quote: Aim for the sky and you'll reach the ceiling. Aim for the ceiling and you'll stay on the floor.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous late-20th-century motivational saying; a close variant appears in the 1998 book 'Prayer for Parish Groups' (Harrington & Kavanagh). Only pinned on Shankly in 2013, 30 years after his death.
candidates.whyNotable: A feel-good motivational line pinned on Shankly in 2013, three decades after his death; Wikiquote flags it Disputed because near-identical sayings circulated anonymously well before any Shankly attribution.

candidates.quote: If you are first you are first. If you are second you are nothing.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitously attributed to Shankly across football sites, but not in his sourced Wikiquote section and no primary citation could be located.

candidates.quote: I must also have a dark side if I am to be whole.
candidates.trueOrigin: Circulated as a paraphrase of Jung's writing on the shadow; Wikiquote lists it under 'Attributed' with no citation to a specific work.
candidates.whyNotable: A popular 'shadow work' quote-card attributed to Jung that Wikiquote carries only as unsourced/attributed rather than verified.

candidates.quote: Show me a sane man and I will cure him for you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attribution is contested (also pinned on Freud, Guy Bellamy, and Jolande Jacobi), but Quote Investigator concludes Jung probably did say it, based on Jolande Jacobi's testimony recorded by Vincent Brome.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely shared aphorism whose authorship is genuinely disputed across several figures; QI investigates and leans toward Jung as the real source.

candidates.quote: Elegance is refusal.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous; popularized by Diana Vreeland in her 1980 book 'Allure,' though Vreeland explicitly said she did not know who originated it.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous fashion-caption line pinned on Chanel; QI found no evidence she ever said it and traces its popularity to Diana Vreeland, who herself disclaimed authorship, leaving the true origin anonymous.

candidates.quote: Nature gives you the face you have at twenty; it is up to you to merit the face you have at fifty.
candidates.trueOrigin: An older proverb about deserving one's face; earliest anchor an 1891 anecdote crediting Edwin M. Stanton ('A man of fifty is responsible for his face'). A three-part version was credited to Chanel in September 1938 Paris Vogue.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely shared 'wisdom' quote; QI shows the responsible-for-your-face idea circulated since at least the 1880s (traced to Edwin M. Stanton) and was credited to George Orwell, Mae West, and others, making Chanel a late adopter rather than the originator.

candidates.quote: If you think you are too small to make a difference, try sleeping with a mosquito.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest documented use attributed to Anita Roddick (Time, Jan 1993); no genuine Dalai Lama source, often relabeled an African proverb.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitously captioned as a Dalai Lama or 'African proverb' line, but Wikiquote's earliest trace is a 1993 Time magazine attribution to Anita Roddick, with Dalai Lama credits only appearing from 2004.

candidates.quote: A woman is like a tea bag; you never know how strong it is until it's in hot water.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Roosevelt source; a similar remark was attributed to Nancy Reagan in 1981.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral 'empowerment' line constantly credited to Roosevelt, but Wikiquote finds no original source and notes a closely related quip attributed to Nancy Reagan in 1981.

candidates.quote: Yesterday is history, tomorrow is a mystery, and today is a gift, that's why they call it the present.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified originator; QI documents anonymous earlier variants of the 'present/gift' wordplay with no link to Roosevelt.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous inspirational line attributed to Roosevelt (and others, e.g. Kung Fu Panda); QI finds no genuine Roosevelt source and traces the saying to anonymous earlier wordplay.

candidates.quote: You must learn from the mistakes of others. You can't possibly live long enough to make them all yourself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous folk saying circulating by the 1940s; the attribution to Roosevelt appeared much later.
candidates.whyNotable: Folk-wisdom aphorism attributed to Roosevelt, but QI traces it to 1940s sources circulating without her name and finds the Roosevelt ascription is a later addition.

candidates.quote: Human beings hide their feelings, but a cat does not.
candidates.trueOrigin: A rough paraphrase of 'People hide their feelings for various reasons, but cats never do,' known only anecdotally through family/biographer channels rather than any published Hemingway text.
candidates.whyNotable: Beloved cat-lover quote Wikiquote flags as an unsourced paraphrase.

candidates.quote: I love sleep. My life has the tendency to fall apart when I'm awake, you know?
candidates.trueOrigin: No source in Hemingway's published work; Wikiquote notes it may originate from a 2000 post in the alt.support.depression Usenet group.
candidates.whyNotable: Popular relatable 'Hemingway' quote with no basis in his writing.

candidates.quote: Few people think more than two or three times a year; I have made an international reputation for myself by thinking once or twice a week.
candidates.trueOrigin: Credited to Shaw via 1933 Reader's Digest; primary Shaw source not established
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently quoted as vintage Shaw; QI traces its spread to a 1933 Reader's Digest attribution without a solid earlier Shaw source.

candidates.quote: If you want to tell people the truth, make them laugh, otherwise they'll kill you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Popular wording unverified; possibly derived from Shaw's John Bull's Other Island (1907): 'My way of joking is to tell the truth...'
candidates.whyNotable: Widely credited to Shaw (and to Wilde, Chaplin, and W. C. Fields); QI notes it may be a compression of Shaw's real line in John Bull's Other Island but the popular wording is unverified.

candidates.quote: The longer I live, the more I am inclined to the belief that this earth is used by other planets as a lunatic asylum.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attribution to Shaw unverified; QI documents variant forms without a firm primary source
candidates.whyNotable: A widely circulated quip attributed to Shaw; QI examines the attribution and finds the citation trail thin and unsettled.

candidates.quote: It is too probable that no plan we propose will be adopted. Perhaps another dreadful conflict is to be sustained.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Washington at the Constitutional Convention (25 May 1787) but uncorroborated in Madison's notes; authenticity contested (Bancroft accepted it, Lodge argued against).
candidates.whyNotable: Inscribed at the Department of Commerce, the Washington Square arch, and Constitution Hall as Washington's words at the 1787 Constitutional Convention, yet it is absent from Madison's convention records and rejected by historians like Henry Cabot Lodge.

candidates.quote: It is well enough that people of the nation do not understand our banking and monetary system, for if they did, I believe there would be a revolution before tomorrow morning.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase introduced by Rep. Charles Binderup (1937); no direct Ford source, though Ford wrote against finance dominance in My Life and Work.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial conspiracy/finance meme attributed to Ford; Wikiquote notes it originates as a 1937 paraphrase by Congressman Charles Binderup, not a documented Ford quote.

candidates.quote: In everyone's life, at some time, our inner fire goes out. It is then burst into flame by an encounter with another human being. We should all be thankful for those people who rekindle the inner spirit.
candidates.trueOrigin: Albert Schweitzer — from his 1924 memoir 'Aus meiner Kindheit und Jugendzeit' (Memoirs of Childhood and Youth), translated by C. T. Campion; Valvano quoted/paraphrased it in the late 1980s and it is now frequently pinned on Valvano himself.
candidates.whyNotable: A signature 'Valvano' inspirational line that Quote Investigator traces to Albert Schweitzer's 1924 memoir; Valvano only popularized a paraphrase (Daily News 1989, his 1991 autobiography), so it is commonly misattributed to him.

candidates.quote: If you fail to prepare, you are preparing to fail.
candidates.trueOrigin: An older proverb; Wooden used the expression in a 1977 Texas Tech speech but did not coin it. QI also finds it linked to Benjamin Franklin, Robert H. Schuller, and various 19th-century figures.
candidates.whyNotable: The polished variant of Wooden's most-attributed maxim; QI shows the saying predates his usage and is spread across many claimed authors.

candidates.quote: Things turn out best for the people who make the best of the way things turn out.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wooden included it in a 1973 book he co-authored but did not claim coinage or give an ascription; QI traces the idea to earlier figures including Art Linkletter.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of Wooden motivational-poster culture, but QI shows he used it without claiming authorship and that it circulated before him.

candidates.quote: Show me a good and gracious loser, and I'll show you a failure
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous proverb; concept dates to at least 1904, exact wording variants emerge 1943 (Rockne credit) and 1962-1965 (Doerner, Auerbach)
candidates.whyNotable: A famous 'good loser' put-down credited to Rockne since a 1943 attribution, but QI finds the saying is anonymous and has been pinned on Red Auerbach, Vince Lombardi, Robert Zuppke, Nixon and others with no proof Rockne originated it.

candidates.quote: Everything negative — pressure, challenges — is all an opportunity for me to rise.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified — credited to Bryant since 2005 with no primary source; also picked up by NBA player Hasheem Thabeet by 2009 after it was already circulating.
candidates.whyNotable: Kobe's single most-shared motivational line, but Quote Investigator found the earliest attribution in a 2005 Pennsylvania celebrities cookbook with no citation and never located a speech, interview, or article where Bryant actually said it.

candidates.quote: When I let go of what I am, I become what I might be.
candidates.trueOrigin: Modern interpretive paraphrase of the Tao Te Ching; not a faithful translation of Laozi
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular 'letting go' line quoted as pure Lao Tzu; it derives from modern interpretive translations of the Tao Te Ching rather than a literal rendering of the original text.

candidates.quote: There is no room in baseball for discrimination. It is our national pastime and a game for all.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulates as Gehrig's stand against segregated baseball, but even ESPN flags it only as 'widely attributed,' with no located primary record.

candidates.quote: He who lives in harmony with himself lives in harmony with the universe.
candidates.trueOrigin: Appears in Dan Millman's 1995 'The Life You Were Born to Live'; no confirmed Meditations source, likely a modern paraphrase.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared as Stoic wisdom, but Wikiquote lists it as unverified - it surfaces in Dan Millman's 1995 self-help book with no confirmed source in the Meditations.

candidates.quote: But suppose the child inherited my beauty and your brains?
candidates.trueOrigin: A floating joke that predates Monroe by decades, told earlier about George Bernard Shaw, Isadora Duncan, and others.
candidates.whyNotable: The famous 'beauty and brains' comeback (often set as a Monroe-and-Einstein or Monroe-and-Bernard-Shaw exchange); QI shows the joke circulated long before Monroe and is a floating anecdote.

candidates.quote: There are three kinds of lies: lies, damned lies, and statistics.
candidates.trueOrigin: Twain attributed it to Benjamin Disraeli; actual coiner is unconfirmed (various late-19th-century candidates).
candidates.whyNotable: Twain popularized and helped spread this line but himself credited it to Benjamin Disraeli; the true originator remains disputed.

candidates.quote: The old law of an eye for an eye leaves everybody blind.
candidates.trueOrigin: Proverb of indefinite origin, variously attributed to Gandhi and others; no verified King source.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely credited to King (and used in Spike Lee's 'Do the Right Thing') but the underlying 'eye for an eye leaves everybody blind' proverb has no firm origin and is also pinned on Gandhi.

candidates.quote: To be a Christian without prayer is no more possible than to be alive without breathing.
candidates.trueOrigin: First attributed to King by George Sweeting (Moody Church) in 1979; no earlier documentation.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared as King, but Wikiquote finds no source earlier than pastor George Sweeting's 1979 book, casting doubt on the attribution.

candidates.quote: Poetry is music written for the human voice.
candidates.trueOrigin: Angelou attributed it to her mentor Bertha Flowers, not to herself.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently attributed to Angelou, but she herself credited the expression to her mentor Bertha Flowers, so the popular attribution is a reassignment.

candidates.quote: I'm so fast that last night I turned off the light switch in my hotel room and was in bed before the room was dark
candidates.trueOrigin: Older 'in bed before the room was dark' joke; earlier tied to Satchel Paige and vaudeville
candidates.whyNotable: One of Ali's signature speed boasts, but QI shows the light-switch joke is an older vaudeville gag also told by Satchel Paige before Ali used it.

candidates.quote: An army marches on its stomach
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified source; earliest attributions post-date Napoleon by decades, also credited to Frederick the Great.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-pinned Napoleon lines; QI finds no contemporaneous source and shows the credit appeared decades after his death, also attributed to Frederick the Great.

candidates.quote: Imagination rules the world
candidates.trueOrigin: Ascribed to Napoleon by Las Cases from an 1816 conversation; possibly derived from Blaise Pascal.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently cited as Napoleon's; QI notes it rests on a secondhand 1816 conversation recorded by Las Cases and may echo Pascal.

candidates.quote: Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake
candidates.trueOrigin: No reliable primary source; QI finds only a loosely related paraphrase in an 1836 history.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely shared strategy quip; QI could find no solid Napoleon source and only a loosely similar remark in an 1836 history book.

candidates.quote: There is not a single citizen in South Africa who is not ready to stand by his Palestinian brothers in their legitimate fight against the Zionist racists.
candidates.trueOrigin: Circulated via Mathaba.net with no verified primary source; Wikiquote lists it as disputed and the wording does not match any authenticated Mandela statement.
candidates.whyNotable: The sole entry in Wikiquote's Disputed section for Mandela; politically charged and lacks a verified source, so flag for editorial judgment before building.

candidates.quote: I do not think there is any thrill that can go through the human heart like that felt by the inventor as he sees some creation of the brain unfolding to success...Such emotions make a man forget food, sleep, friends, love, everything.
candidates.trueOrigin: Echoes sentiments in Tesla's 1919 'My Inventions' but the exact wording is attested only via a 2008 secondary source.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely reproduced inspirational Tesla passage; Wikiquote lists it under Attributed, sourced to a 2008 popular book rather than a verified Tesla original.

candidates.quote: If you want to find the secrets of the universe, think in terms of energy, frequency and vibration.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Tesla source; traced only to a secondhand claim by purple-plate promoter Ralph Bergstresser.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared 'Tesla' quote on social media; Wikiquote lists it as Disputed with its only source being Ralph Bergstresser, who claimed to have heard it from Tesla in person with no documentary backing.

candidates.quote: A pessimist is one who, when he has the choice of two evils, chooses both.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unattributed until 1977; similar formulations appear from 1899 onward with no link to Wilde.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared definition of a pessimist credited to Wilde, but Wikiquote finds no attribution to him until 1977.

candidates.quote: I don't want to go to heaven. None of my friends are there.
candidates.trueOrigin: No known source in Wilde's writings; Wikiquote notes the attribution circulating via Goodreads-era social sharing with no citation.
candidates.whyNotable: Popular irreverent one-liner with no documented Wilde source; a classic quote-card fabrication.

candidates.quote: I have nothing to declare except my genius.
candidates.trueOrigin: Apocryphal customs anecdote; QI notes the earliest citation is 1910, nearly two decades after the supposed 1882 incident and a decade after Wilde's death.
candidates.whyNotable: The iconic 'customs official' quip; QI rates the evidence weak because it first surfaces long after the event and after Wilde had died.

candidates.quote: Some cause happiness wherever they go; others whenever they go.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous; QI finds it in an insurance magazine (1908) and traces the Wilde attribution to a possible misreading of a 1947 aphorism collection.
candidates.whyNotable: Beloved back-handed insult attributed to Wilde; QI finds no evidence he ever used it and pins the earliest instance to an anonymous 1908 source.

candidates.quote: True friends stab you in the front.
candidates.trueOrigin: No Wilde source; earliest instances tied to Walter Winchell (1955) and others; Wilde attribution only began circa 1989.
candidates.whyNotable: Edgy friendship aphorism commonly tagged Wilde; Wikiquote finds no source before the mid-20th century, long after his death.

candidates.quote: I do not seek. I find.
candidates.trueOrigin: Spanish 'Yo no busco, yo encuentro'; quoted in Graham Sutherland's 1936 essay 'A Trend in English Draughtsmanship' but the direct attribution to Picasso is disputed.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous aphoristic Picasso line whose earliest sighting is a 1936 essay by Graham Sutherland, with Wikiquote flagging the direct attribution as disputed.

candidates.quote: Inspiration exists, but it has to find you working.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Picasso only in a 1994 publication (Spanish: 'La inspiración existe, pero tiene que encontrarte trabajando'); no contemporaneous source in Picasso's own words is documented.
candidates.whyNotable: A studio-motivation staple credited to Picasso, but the earliest documented attribution is a 1994 posthumous source with no primary record.

candidates.quote: It took me four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child.
candidates.trueOrigin: Only appears in print from 1998, posthumously; multiple variant wordings exist ('At eight I was Raphael...') and no contemporaneous primary source is documented.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular Picasso maxim that surfaces only in posthumous 1998 sources with shifting wording, so Wikiquote treats it as unverified.

candidates.quote: A penalty is a cowardly way to score.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown — no cited source on Wikiquote.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently quoted as Pelé's view on penalty kicks, but Wikiquote lists it without any source — a searchable, quotable line whose provenance is unconfirmed.

candidates.quote: The more difficult the victory, the greater the happiness in winning.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown — no cited source; provenance unverified.
candidates.whyNotable: Very widely circulated as a Pelé quote on sports/motivation sites, but Wikiquote carries it with no source attached — a popular line with no verified provenance.

candidates.quote: Successful people never worry about what others are doing.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source in any of Plato's works; earliest occurrence is a 2011 tweet.
candidates.whyNotable: A modern motivational-meme line credited to Plato that Wikiquote traces only to a 2011 tweet.

candidates.quote: The highest form of pure thought is in mathematics.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source in Plato's writings; earliest example found on Google Books is a 1990 Usenet post.
candidates.whyNotable: A commonly-quoted 'Plato' line on math and reason that Wikiquote can trace no earlier than a 1990 Usenet post.

candidates.quote: Wise men speak because they have something to say; fools because they have to say something.
candidates.trueOrigin: Cannot be found complete in Plato's writings; likely a conflation of passages from the Symposium and Laches.
candidates.whyNotable: An extremely popular 'Plato' aphorism Wikiquote flags as unverifiable, likely stitched together from separate dialogues.

candidates.quote: Politicians are like diapers. They need to be changed regularly, and for the same reason.
candidates.trueOrigin: No support for Mark Twain; earliest documented version is a 1966 newspaper column by Dick Nolan (San Francisco Examiner), evolved from older 'change your socks/politicians' jokes. Robin Williams merely voiced a version in Man of the Year (2006), screenplay by Barry Levinson.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral 'politician' one-liner popularly pinned on Mark Twain and often re-credited to Robin Williams because he delivered it in the 2006 film Man of the Year; QI finds no Twain evidence and traces the earliest match to a 1966 Dick Nolan column in the San Francisco Examiner.

candidates.quote: The problem is not that people are taxed too little, the problem is that government spends too much.
candidates.trueOrigin: Listed by Wikiquote as merely attributed; earliest sourcing points to Richard A. Viguerie's book 'Conservatives Betrayed' (p. 43) rather than a primary Reagan speech.
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly reproduced as a Reagan tax quote, yet Wikiquote can only source it to a secondary book, not to Reagan himself.

candidates.quote: And those who were seen dancing were thought to be insane by those who could not hear the music.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous/proverbial; earliest precursor Anne Louise Germaine de Staël, De l'Allemagne (1813); modern phrasing popularized by George Carlin's Brain Droppings (1997), later credited by him to 'Anon.' Not from Rumi or Nietzsche.
candidates.whyNotable: Massively shared, credited to both Rumi and Nietzsche; QI finds no evidence for either and calls it anonymous, with a Germaine de Staël precursor (1813) and George Carlin popularizing the modern wording in 1997.

candidates.quote: Everyone has been made for some particular work, and the desire for that work has been put in every heart.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary Rumi source established; earliest citation is a modern secondary work (Jan Phillips, Marry Your Muse, 1997).
candidates.whyNotable: A common graduation- and career-inspiration 'Rumi' line, but Wikiquote can source it only to a 1997 creativity self-help book (Jan Phillips, Marry Your Muse), not to Rumi's works.

candidates.quote: Let the beauty of what you love be what you do.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary Rumi source established; earliest citation is a modern secondary compilation (Linda J. Ferguson, Path for Greatness: Spirituality at Work, 2000).
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared 'Rumi' lines on social media and tattoos, but Wikiquote can source it only to a 2000 self-help book (Linda J. Ferguson, Path for Greatness), not to any of Rumi's actual works.

candidates.quote: We are all broken. That's how the light gets in.
candidates.trueOrigin: No single author; a modern paraphrase-blend of Ernest Hemingway (A Farewell to Arms, 1929) and Leonard Cohen ('Anthem', 1992), with conceptual precursors in Emerson (1841) and Benjamin Blood (1860). Not from Rumi.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral inspirational line pinned variously on Rumi, Hemingway, and Leonard Cohen; QI finds no real source and traces it to a 2013-era social-media blend of Hemingway's 1929 'the world breaks everyone' and Cohen's 1992 'there is a crack in everything, that's how the light gets in.'

candidates.quote: Wherever you stand, be the soul of that place.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary Rumi source established; earliest citation is a modern secondary work (Patricia Flasch, Becoming a Love Dog, 2009).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely reposted 'Rumi' aphorism whose only citation on Wikiquote is a 2009 book (Patricia Flasch, Becoming a Love Dog), not any verified Rumi text.

candidates.quote: You were born with wings. Why prefer to crawl through life?
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary Rumi source established; earliest citation is a modern compilation (Larry Chang, Wisdom for the Soul, 2006).
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous feel-good 'Rumi' quote across Instagram and posters, but Wikiquote traces it only to a 2006 quotation anthology (Larry Chang, Wisdom for the Soul), with no link to Rumi's documented writings.

candidates.quote: Don't pray when it rains if you don't pray when the sun shines.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Paige via a 1959 AP column, but QI notes it is also credited to evangelist Billy Sunday and columnist Hal Boyle — a shared/contested credit rather than a clean Paige original.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely quoted as pure Paige, but QI documents competing credits to Billy Sunday and Hal Boyle, making the origin genuinely disputed.

candidates.quote: Build your opponent a golden bridge to retreat across.
candidates.trueOrigin: A paraphrase blending Sun Tzu's 'leave a way of escape' with later commentary (Tu Mu); the 'golden bridge' phrasing is not in Sun Tzu's own words.
candidates.whyNotable: A vivid maxim credited to Sun Tzu that Wikiquote lists as disputed — it dresses up his 'leave an outlet' principle in words he never wrote.

candidates.quote: Victory is reserved for those who are willing to pay its price.
candidates.trueOrigin: Does not appear in The Art of War; Wikiquote lists it as disputed with no located source, possibly a modern/anime misattribution.
candidates.whyNotable: A heavily-shared 'Sun Tzu' motivational line Wikiquote flags as disputed and unlocated in any translation.

candidates.quote: Baseball is the only field of endeavor where a man can succeed three times out of ten and be considered a good performer.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared inspirational baseball lines pinned on Williams, yet Wikiquote lists it as Unsourced with no primary citation and it circulates attributed to multiple figures.

candidates.quote: By the time you know what to do, you're too old to do it.
candidates.whyNotable: A clever aphorism heavily attributed to Williams but unsourced on Wikiquote; the general form floats among several athletes and comedians, a classic reassignment risk.

candidates.quote: God gets you to the plate, but once you're there you're on your own.
candidates.whyNotable: A feel-good line widely circulated as Williams wisdom on quote sites, but it appears only in Wikiquote's Unsourced list with no located origin.

candidates.quote: Golf is the only sport where the ball doesn't move until you hit it.
candidates.whyNotable: A quippy line commonly credited to Williams yet unsourced; the same observation is attributed to many golfers and comics, so the Williams credit is doubtful.

candidates.quote: Hitting a baseball — I've said it a thousand times — is the single most difficult thing to do in sport.
candidates.whyNotable: Williams genuinely championed this idea, but the exact wording varies wildly across sources and this version sits in Wikiquote's Unsourced list rather than any primary text.

candidates.quote: I'd have been a .290 hitter without a Louisville Slugger.
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently repeated Williams line crediting his bat, but Wikiquote carries it only as Unsourced with no primary citation.

candidates.quote: I've found that you don't need to wear a necktie if you can hit.
candidates.whyNotable: A characterful Williams one-liner about his disdain for formality, popular on quote sites but unsourced on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: The only thing dumber than a pitcher is two pitchers.
candidates.whyNotable: A punchy insult-joke repeated as a Williams zinger but with no source on Wikiquote; the format is a common recycled baseball gag.

candidates.quote: They invented the All-Star game for Willie Mays.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous tribute line credited to Williams and widely quoted, yet it appears only in Wikiquote's Unsourced section without a located origin.

candidates.quote: A man who has never gone to school may steal from a freight car; but if he has a university education, he may steal the whole railroad.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; earliest citation is a 1952 book (William Joseph Grace, 'Art of Communicating Ideas'), decades after Roosevelt's death, with no contemporaneous source.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-circulated zinger about education and corruption credited to TR; Wikiquote lists it as disputed with only a much-later 1952 secondhand citation and no Roosevelt primary source.

candidates.quote: A thorough knowledge of the Bible is worth more than a college education.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; earliest citation is 'Stepping Stones: The Complete Bible Narratives' (1941), with no contemporaneous Roosevelt source.
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently-shared line in religious and inspirational contexts attributed to TR; Wikiquote flags it as disputed, with only a 1941 secondhand quotation and no Roosevelt primary source.

candidates.quote: When they call the roll in the Senate, the Senators do not know whether to answer 'Present' or 'Not Guilty'.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; no primary source ties the line to Roosevelt, and Wikiquote carries it without any sourced citation.
candidates.whyNotable: A recurring political-corruption quip attributed to TR; Wikiquote lists it as disputed with no reliable source establishing Roosevelt as the author.

candidates.quote: Hell, there are no rules here. We're trying to accomplish something.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed via Martin André Rosanoff, Harper's Magazine (1932); original dialect version 'Hell! there ain't no rules around here! We are tryin' to accomplish somep'n!'
candidates.whyNotable: A beloved innovation-culture quote; QI rates it only 'probable,' resting on a single second-hand account (Rosanoff, Harper's Magazine 1932) of a remark from around 1903.

candidates.quote: I'd put my money on the sun and solar energy. What a source of power! I hope we don't have to wait until oil and coal run out before we tackle that.
candidates.trueOrigin: Reported second-hand in James D. Newton, Uncommon Friends (1987); reliability unverified.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitous in renewable-energy messaging; QI notes it comes only from James Newton's 1987 book Uncommon Friends, recalling a 1931 conversation over 50 years later with no archived diary to verify it.

candidates.quote: Non-violence leads to the highest ethics, which is the goal of all evolution.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; first documented in The A-V Magazine (1981).
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared in vegetarian/animal-rights circles as an Edison line, but Wikiquote finds no source earlier than The A-V Magazine (1981) despite claims of an 1890 origin.

candidates.quote: I have recently been examining all the known superstitions of the world, and do not find in our particular superstition one redeeming feature.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; sourced only to an unlocated letter cited by John E. Remsburg (Six Historic Americans, 1906); Monticello scholars consider it unreliable
candidates.whyNotable: A favorite anti-religion Jefferson quote; Wikiquote and the Jefferson Foundation deem it spurious — it rests on an unlocated "letter to Dr. Woods" cited by John Remsburg in 1906 that no one has ever verified.

candidates.quote: It's déjà vu all over again.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; Berra claimed it (about back-to-back Mantle/Maris homers) but no early sourcing supports him
candidates.whyNotable: Perhaps the single most-shared Yogi-ism, yet Wikiquote lists it as disputed: the earliest published attribution to Berra is 1984 and a similar line appears in a 1962 Jim Prior poem, so QI treats it as unverified.

candidates.quote: The most rewarding things you do in life are often the ones that look like they cannot be done
candidates.trueOrigin: Likely Arnold Palmer — QI found no competing ascription — but the earliest evidence is indirect: an August 1966 speech by U.S. Steel president Leslie B. Worthington who credited Palmer, not Palmer's own words.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely reshared motivational line often doubted as a 'fake Palmer' quote; QI actually leans toward it being genuine but flags that only indirect second-hand sourcing exists.

candidates.quote: Our homes are our prisons; let us find freedom in their decoration.
candidates.trueOrigin: From the 1938 Chanel-credited Vogue maxims; possibly derived from or co-written by Pierre Reverdy.
candidates.whyNotable: A design-blog favorite attributed to Chanel; QI ties it to the same 1938 Vogue maxims collection that poet Pierre Reverdy may have authored, so Chanel's sole authorship is unconfirmed.

candidates.quote: The only beautiful eyes are those that look at us tenderly.
candidates.trueOrigin: Published under Chanel's name in Paris Vogue, September 1938, but the maxims may have been ghost-composed by poet Pierre Reverdy.
candidates.whyNotable: A romantic line shared as pure Chanel; QI confirms it appeared in Chanel's September 1938 Vogue maxims but notes a biography suggests poet Pierre Reverdy may have actually composed the maxims, clouding authorship.

candidates.quote: Always do sober what you said you'd do drunk. That will teach you to keep your mouth shut.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI found substantive evidence this originated with Hemingway (in a 1950s letter to publisher Charles Scribner IV), first published by Malcolm Forbes in 1961 — though the precise wording is uncertain and it is frequently conflated with the fabricated 'Write drunk, edit sober.'
candidates.whyNotable: Credibly Hemingway per QI, yet constantly garbled into the fake 'write drunk, edit sober' — a useful page to disambiguate the two.

candidates.quote: The first draft of anything is shit.
candidates.trueOrigin: First published in Arnold Samuelson's 1984 posthumous memoir 'With Hemingway,' recounting a 1930s conversation; no contemporaneous documentation exists, so the exact wording is unverified.
candidates.whyNotable: The go-to writing-advice quote; QI can only trace it to a student's memoir published 23 years after Hemingway's death.

candidates.quote: The most painful thing is losing yourself in the process of loving someone too much, and forgetting that you are special too.
candidates.trueOrigin: Often cited to 'Men Without Women' but appears nowhere in it; Wikiquote traces it to a 2011 blog post by Marc Chernoff, '30 Things to Stop Doing to Yourself.'
candidates.whyNotable: Heavily shared romantic 'Hemingway' quote that is actually a 2011 self-help blog line.

candidates.quote: What lies behind us and what lies before us are tiny matters compared to what lies within us.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry Stanley Haskins, Meditations in Wall Street (1940)
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared inspirational lines pinned on Thoreau (and Emerson); Quote Investigator traces it to Wall Street trader Henry Stanley Haskins in his 1940 book Meditations in Wall Street.

candidates.quote: I don't give advice; I give opinions.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wooden did say a version in Feb 1994 ('I don't like to give advice... I can give an opinion. That's a big difference'), but QI finds the tidy epigram's origin murky, also linked to Bill Walton and Joyce Fittro.
candidates.whyNotable: A pithy line widely quoted as vintage Wooden; QI confirms he expressed the idea but the polished one-liner form has an unclear origin.

candidates.quote: Care about what other people think and you will always be their prisoner.
candidates.trueOrigin: Stephen Mitchell's interpretive translation of the Tao Te Ching (1988), Ch.9; not a faithful rendering of Laozi's words
candidates.whyNotable: Shared endlessly as a direct Lao Tzu quote, but it is Stephen Mitchell's loose 1988 rendering of Tao Te Ching Ch.9, not a literal translation of the original text.

candidates.quote: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.
candidates.trueOrigin: Clare Boothe Luce, 'Stuffed Shirts' (1931) for the early form; Leonard Thiessen (1946) for the modern phrasing. Earliest da Vinci attribution only around 2000.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitous design-world maxim pinned on Leonardo (and popularized by Apple's 1977 marketing); QI and Wikiquote find no da Vinci source and credit Clare Boothe Luce (1931, 'the height of sophistication is simplicity') and Leonard Thiessen (1946).

candidates.quote: Hollywood is a place where they'll pay you a thousand dollars for a kiss and fifty cents for your soul.
candidates.trueOrigin: First printed in Monroe's posthumous 1974 autobiography 'My Story' (published 12 years after her death); authenticity of the wording is contested.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-quoted 'cynical Hollywood' Monroe lines; QI finds it only in her ghostwritten posthumous 1974 autobiography 'My Story,' so whether she actually said it is uncertain.

candidates.quote: Everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth
candidates.trueOrigin: Tyson said the earlier form 'Everybody has plans until they get hit for the first time' (AP, Aug 1987); the underlying idea predates him in Helmuth von Moltke the Elder (1871). Sometimes reassigned to Joe Louis, which QI calls late and poorly supported.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-quoted lines on the internet; QI credits Tyson but shows the viral 'punched in the mouth/face' wording is a paraphrase of what he actually said, and the concept has military antecedents.

candidates.quote: God is really only another artist. He invented the giraffe, the elephant and the cat. He has no real style. He just goes on trying other things.
candidates.trueOrigin: Reported secondhand by Francoise Gilot in her 1964 memoir 'Life with Picasso', where she recounts hearing it from Picasso in the 1940s; no direct primary record exists.
candidates.whyNotable: Credibly credited but only through Gilot's 1964 memoir recollection, so it sits between genuine and unverified rather than fully sourced.

candidates.quote: When painters get together they talk about where you can buy the best turpentine.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest evidence located by QI is a 1966 book by screenwriter/director Garson Kanin, who ascribed the words to Picasso; no earlier primary source is documented.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-quoted Picasso quip about artists talking shop, but QI can only trace it to a secondhand 1966 anecdote by Garson Kanin.

candidates.quote: If your house was burning and you could only take one thing with you, what would it be? I would take the fire.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jean Cocteau, in 1951 radio interviews with Andre Fraigneau (published in Entretiens, 1965/1988); Coelho retold it in 2007
candidates.whyNotable: A poetic line that circulates as a Coelho quote; QI shows Coelho was only a transmitter who shared the anecdote on his website in 2007, while the actual remark is Jean Cocteau's from 1951 radio interviews.

candidates.quote: The strength of the team is each individual member. The strength of each member is the team.
candidates.trueOrigin: Phil Jackson's own phrasing, closely echoing Rudyard Kipling's 'For the strength of the pack is the wolf, and the strength of the wolf is the pack'
candidates.whyNotable: Jackson's most-circulated leadership line is genuinely his wording, but a near-direct adaptation of Kipling's wolf-pack couplet.

candidates.quote: The first human who hurled an insult instead of a stone was the founder of civilization.
candidates.trueOrigin: Freud repeated the aphorism but attributed it to an unnamed English writer; true originator undetermined.
candidates.whyNotable: Often quoted as pure Freud, but QI shows Freud himself credited the idea to an unnamed English writer, so he popularized rather than originated it.

candidates.quote: There has always been a saying in baseball that you can't make a hitter, but I think you can improve a hitter. More than you can improve a fielder.
candidates.whyNotable: Reflects Williams' teaching from The Science of Hitting and is often quoted as his, but Wikiquote lists this wording as Unsourced rather than tying it to the book.

candidates.quote: You may not realize it when it happens, but a kick in the teeth may be the best thing in the world for you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rooted in authentic Disney interview statements (he used 'kick in the pants' in a 1956 Saturday Evening Post interview); the 'kick in the teeth' phrasing appeared in the 1957 biography The Story of Walt Disney.
candidates.whyNotable: A popular Disney resilience quote; QI finds Disney genuinely expressed the idea in 1950s interviews but as a 'kick in the pants' — the 'teeth' wording comes from his 1957 biography.

candidates.quote: Change the way you look at things, and the things you look at change.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wayne Dyer, who included the line in his 2004 book The Power of Intention. QI found no substantive evidence for the popular Max Planck attribution — that error likely arose because Dyer tied the idea to quantum physics, and Planck was the famous quantum theorist.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous 'quantum' inspirational quote falsely pinned on physicist Max Planck; QI credits it to Wayne Dyer's 2004 The Power of Intention.

candidates.quote: We are not human beings having a spiritual experience. We are spiritual beings having a human experience.
candidates.trueOrigin: Wayne W. Dyer is QI's most-likely originator (a version appeared in a 1988 Time magazine ad of his writing; the exact statement is in his 1989 book You'll See It When You Believe It). No instance has been found in Teilhard de Chardin's actual works; Stephen Covey's Teilhard attribution appears to have spread the error.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared spiritual quotes on the internet, near-universally credited to Teilhard de Chardin — but QI traces it back to Wayne Dyer himself, making Dyer the real author of a line pinned on a French philosopher-priest.

candidates.quote: If people don't want to come to the ballpark, how are you going to stop them?
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to impresario Sol Hurok in 1952; linked to Berra in 1962
candidates.whyNotable: Often quoted as pure Berra, but Wikiquote records it was originally attributed to impresario Sol Hurok in 1952 and only linked to Berra in 1962.

candidates.quote: Ninety percent of this game is half-mental.
candidates.trueOrigin: First attributed to outfielder Jim Wohlford, April 1974
candidates.whyNotable: A beloved 'Yogi math' line, but Wikiquote notes the phrasing was first attributed in April 1974 to reserve outfielder Jim Wohlford, not Berra.

candidates.quote: Attitude is a little thing that makes a big difference.
candidates.trueOrigin: Popularized via Ziglar's 'See You at the Top' (1977); also widely misattributed to Winston Churchill and Theodore Roosevelt.
candidates.whyNotable: Contested between Ziglar (who wrote a matching line in 'See You at the Top,' 1977) and Winston Churchill; QI treats the modern one-liner as a shared/evolving adage rather than clearly either man's.

candidates.quote: A quotation is a handy thing to have about, saving one the trouble of thinking for oneself, always a laborious business.
candidates.trueOrigin: A. A. Milne, essay 'The Record Lie' in the 1920 collection If I May (QI notes Dorothy L. Sayers later voiced a similar, separate line via Lord Peter Wimsey in 1932).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, oft-quoted Milne aphorism that QI confirms and sources precisely, making a good real anchor amid the fakes.

candidates.quote: It is hard to be brave when you're only a Very Small Animal.
candidates.trueOrigin: A. A. Milne, Winnie-the-Pooh (1926), Chapter Seven (Piglet).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Piglet line from the original Winnie-the-Pooh, sourced on Wikiquote by chapter, useful as a verified anchor.

candidates.quote: when you are a Bear of Very Little Brain, and you Think of Things, you find sometimes that a Thing which seemed very Thingish inside you is quite different when it gets out into the open and has other people looking at it.
candidates.trueOrigin: A. A. Milne, The House at Pooh Corner (1928), Chapter Six (Pooh).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, widely quoted Pooh passage sourced on Wikiquote to The House at Pooh Corner, serving as a real anchor beside the misattributions.

candidates.quote: A house divided against itself cannot stand.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely delivered by Lincoln in his 'House Divided' speech accepting the Illinois Republican Senate nomination, Springfield, June 16, 1858 (Lincoln himself drew the phrase from the Gospels).
candidates.whyNotable: A real, well-sourced Lincoln line that anchors the hub against the debunks; famous framing of a nation half-slave and half-free.

candidates.quote: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine opening of the Gettysburg Address, delivered at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery, Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, November 19, 1863.
candidates.whyNotable: The most famous verified Lincoln passage; a real anchor alongside the misattributions.

candidates.quote: All men by nature desire to know.
candidates.trueOrigin: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book I, 980a.21 (genuine)
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, well-sourced Aristotle line and the famous opening of the Metaphysics (Book I, 980a.21) — a real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: Baseball always has been and always will be a game demanding team play. You can have the nine greatest individual ball players in the world, but if they don't play together the club won't be worth a dime.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ruth's; 'Babe Ruth's Own Book of Baseball' (1928), Chapter X (also carried in The Pittsburgh Press, January 18, 1929).
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, well-sourced Ruth line from his own 1928 book, giving the hub a real team-play anchor; cited by Wikiquote to Babe Ruth's Own Book of Baseball (1928), Chapter X.

candidates.quote: I always swing at the ball with all my might. I hit or miss big.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ruth's; Chicago Tribune, August 13, 1920 (as told to Westbrook Pegler), reprinted in 'Playing the Game: My Early Years in Baseball' (2011).
candidates.whyNotable: A verified early Ruth quote captured in his own words, sourced by Wikiquote to the Chicago Tribune (August 13, 1920) as told to Westbrook Pegler.

candidates.quote: Either write something worth reading or do something worth the writing
candidates.trueOrigin: Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack, 1738 edition; assembled by Franklin from two pre-existing sayings.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely Franklin line from the 1738 Poor Richard's Almanack; QI confirms he constructed it, though he built it from two earlier sayings he had encountered.

candidates.quote: In this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely written by Franklin in a Nov 13, 1789 letter to Jean-Baptiste Le Roy; the phrase itself predates him, appearing in Christopher Bullock's 1716 farce 'The Cobler of Preston.'
candidates.whyNotable: Franklin genuinely wrote this in a 1789 letter to Jean-Baptiste Le Roy, but QI shows the death-and-taxes pairing was already circulating decades earlier (e.g., Christopher Bullock's 1716 play), so he popularized rather than coined it.

candidates.quote: Every individual is an exception to the rule.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Jung: appears in his 1925 article 'Psychological Types' (from a 1923 lecture) and his 1928 Contributions to Analytical Psychology; QI notes a similar 1906 remark but credits Jung with popularizing it.
candidates.whyNotable: A real, QI-verified Jung line that anchors the hub; QI traces it to his 1925 article and confirms the attribution.

candidates.quote: Who looks outside, dreams; who looks inside, awakes.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Jung: from a letter to Fanny Bowditch, 22 October 1916 — though it is almost always shared as a rootless caption with no citation.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular poster quote that is actually genuine (1916 letter) but virtually never shared with its real source, making it a strong verify-the-source anchor.

candidates.quote: A man who dares to waste one hour of time has not discovered the value of life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Darwin, attributed in 'The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin' (1887); a genuine but sometimes loosely sourced line.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely Darwin line (from a study of earthworms / recorded in his correspondence) that is widely shared as motivation and has a sourced Wikiquote entry, useful as a real anchor.
