candidates.quote: All we've got is cotton, and slaves and...arrogance.
candidates.trueOrigin: Transcribed verbatim at Wikiquote, spoken by Rhett Butler (Clark Gable) at Twelve Oaks. ORIGINATION: adapted from Margaret Mitchell's 1936 novel, chapter 6, which Wikiquote transcribes as: "Why, all we have is cotton and slaves and arrogance. They'd lick us in a month." The film tightened the novel's sentence; it did not originate the line. Gone with the Wind (1939), Selznick International Pictures, dist. MGM. Screen credit Sidney Howard; writing shared/disputed (Hecht, Selznick, Swerling, Garrett, Keon, Van Druten uncredited).
candidates.whyNotable: The single best-evidenced origination case on this title: both the film wording AND the earlier novel wording are transcribed at Wikiquote, so the film-borrowed-this claim can be cited on both sides from the authority itself rather than inferred. Lower search demand than the others, but the strongest provenance.

candidates.quote: Elementary, my dear Holmes, elementary.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Edwin Blum and William A. Drake for The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (1939), 20th Century Fox. Spoken by Nigel Bruce as Dr. Watson, answering Rathbone's Holmes ('Very effective, my dear Watson!') in the film's closing exchange, after Watson swats a fly Holmes was trying to shoo with his violin. Rights holder is the studio (work-for-hire).
candidates.whyNotable: The film's actual closing beat, and the exact counterweight to the misquote above: what this film demonstrably ends on is Watson INVERTING the catchphrase back onto Holmes, not Holmes delivering it. Wikiquote transcribes it verbatim with both speakers. Load-bearing context for any page asserting what the 1939 film did or did not say.

candidates.quote: Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn.
candidates.trueOrigin: Transcribed verbatim at Wikiquote as the closing line of the film, spoken by Rhett Butler (Clark Gable). Gone with the Wind (1939), Selznick International Pictures, distributed by MGM. ORIGINATION: the film is widely credited with coining this, but the line is adapted from Margaret Mitchell's 1936 novel, where Rhett's line reads "My dear, I don't give a damn" — the film's contribution is the word "Frankly." AUTHORSHIP: sole screen credit to Sidney Howard, but disputed/shared in practice (Hecht, Selznick, Swerling, Garrett, Keon, Van Druten all uncredited; Selznick claimed most of the dialogue).
candidates.whyNotable: AFI #1 of the top 100 movie quotations. Serves as the verified anchor for this title, and carries the origination correction: the film sharpened a novel line rather than inventing one.

candidates.quote: Gentlemen, it's been a privilege flying with you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Apollo 13 (1995), spoken by the Jim Lovell character (Tom Hanks). Screenplay by William Broyles Jr. & Al Reinert (uncredited rewrite by John Sayles); Imagine Entertainment, distributed by Universal Pictures; based on Lost Moon (1994) by Jim Lovell & Jeffrey Kluger. A written screen line, not a transcribed 1970 transmission — the writers are the authors; Lovell is the character, Hanks the actor.
candidates.whyNotable: Transcribed exactly on Wikiquote under Jim Lovell, with no dispute note. Serves as a clean anchor for the title: widely quoted and correctly sourced to the film, so the page asserts no correction. Worth stating plainly that it is a scripted line rather than something the real crew radioed, since this title's whole problem is readers assuming film dialogue is transcript.

candidates.quote: Here's looking at you, kid.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein and Howard Koch — Casablanca (1942), dir. Michael Curtiz, Warner Bros. (work-for-hire; rights holder Warner Bros., not the writers). Spoken by Rick Blaine, played by Humphrey Bogart — the actor is the speaker, not the author. Adapted from the unproduced 1940 play "Everybody Comes to Rick's" by Murray Burnett and Joan Alison; Wikiquote does not establish whether the line originated in the play.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor for the title: sourced exactly on Wikiquote and ranked #5 in AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes. Transcribed in full context ("All right, I will. Here's looking at you, kid.") and repeated in the airport farewell. Useful as a control against the misquotes — this one the public actually gets right, while still misattributing its authorship to Bogart rather than the Epsteins and Koch. (A persistent legend holds Bogart ad-libbed it while teaching Bergman poker between takes; that is NOT documented at Wikiquote or QI and must not be asserted on the page.)

candidates.quote: He's dead, Jim.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine recurring line of Dr. Leonard McCoy (DeForest Kelley) across many Star Trek: The Original Series episodes (Desilu/Paramount for NBC, 1966-69) — e.g. "The Changeling" — with variants "She's dead, Jim" and "It's dead, Jim". As a catchphrase repeated across episodes by different writers it has no single writing credit. Wikiquote records that Kelley had already delivered a near-identical line, "He's dead, Captain", as a military physician in the 1956 film The Man in the Grey Flannel Suit — a decade before Star Trek.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor, and the control case for the "You're dead, Jim" misquote above — pairing them shows readers the exact axis of the error. Wikiquote transcribes it and adds a genuine pre-history: the same actor said essentially the same line in a 1956 film, so even the real catchphrase has an origin story that predates the show.

candidates.quote: I do wish we could chat longer, but I'm having an old friend for dinner.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Ted Tally, adapting Thomas Harris's 1988 novel; spoken by Hannibal Lecter (Anthony Hopkins) in the film's closing scene; The Silence of the Lambs (1991), dir. Jonathan Demme, Orion Pictures (rights holder). Wikiquote transcribes the line with an ellipsis and a closing beat: "I do wish we could chat longer, but … I'm having an old friend for dinner. Bye." — the popular form simply drops the pause and the "Bye", which is compression rather than a misquote. Whether the line originates in Harris's novel or is Tally's for the film is not established here.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor. The film's closing line and one of its two most-quoted; Wikiquote sources it directly. Useful as a contrast case for the two misquote pages — here the public's version is a harmless trim of the transcript, not a rewrite of it, which is precisely the line between compression and misquotation.

candidates.quote: I love you." / "I know.
candidates.trueOrigin: Star Wars: Episode V — The Empire Strikes Back (1980), directed by Irvin Kershner; screenplay credited to Leigh Brackett & Lawrence Kasdan, story by George Lucas. Lucasfilm Ltd. / Twentieth Century-Fox. Leia Organa (Carrie Fisher) / Han Solo (Harrison Ford), in the carbon-freezing chamber. Wikiquote transcribes the exchange exactly as above. AUTHORSHIP EXCEPTION: "I know" was not in the shooting script and did not come from the credited screenwriters. Kershner had settled on a pared-down "I'll be back"; at Harrison Ford's suggestion on set, Han's reply became "I know." This is a rare documented case where the house convention (author = the writer, never the actor) does not resolve cleanly — the line is an on-set contribution by the actor, adopted by the director, and should be recorded as such rather than credited to Brackett or Kasdan.
candidates.whyNotable: Consistently ranked among the best-loved exchanges in film, and heavily searched. Its value to the corpus is the authorship record: the credited screenwriters did not write the famous half of it, which is a real-world stress test of the writer-not-actor rule and worth documenting before someone credits it to Kasdan.

candidates.quote: If you build it, he will come.
candidates.trueOrigin: Originated in W. P. Kinsella's novel Shoeless Joe (Houghton Mifflin, 1982) — spoken by the voice of a ballpark announcer heard by narrator Ray Kinsella. Screenplay by Phil Alden Robinson for Field of Dreams (1989, Universal Pictures), based on Kinsella's novel; Robinson also directed. Spoken on screen by The Voice (credited as "Himself"); heard by Ray Kinsella, played by Kevin Costner. Per house convention the author of the screen line is the writer — but here the line predates the screenplay, so the originating author is Kinsella, and Robinson is the adapter who brought it to screen. Ranked #39 on AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes.
candidates.whyNotable: The anchor for the misquote above: this is the line as actually written and spoken, transcribed exactly at Wikiquote and independently ranked by AFI. Carrying it as its own verified record gives the corpus the correct string alongside the popular wrong one, and lets the page make the "he, not they" contrast concrete. Also carries the borrowed-from-the-novel correction on its own.

candidates.quote: I'll get you, my pretty, and your little dog too!
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line as transcribed, spoken by the Wicked Witch of the West (Margaret Hamilton) to Dorothy. Screenplay by Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson and Edgar Allan Woolf, The Wizard of Oz (1939), Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (rights holder). ORIGINATION: film-original — the Witch has no such line in L. Frank Baum's 1900 novel. AFI ranks it #99 on "100 Years...100 Movie Quotes", rendered identically.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor record, and the necessary counterpart to the "Fly, my pretties" misquote: this is the real line whose singular "my pretty", addressed to Dorothy, gets pluralised and redirected at the flying monkeys in the phantom version. Carrying both lets the two pages cite each other and show exactly where the error comes from. Wording is confirmed by two independent sources (Wikiquote transcription and AFI #99), so 'verified' is safe.

candidates.quote: Let's work the problem, people. Let's not make things any worse by guessing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Apollo 13 (1995), spoken by the Gene Kranz character (Ed Harris). Screenplay by William Broyles Jr. & Al Reinert (uncredited rewrite by John Sayles); Imagine Entertainment, distributed by Universal Pictures. Wikiquote transcribes it with emphasis on "work" and "guessing" (italicised in the source). A written screen line; the writers are the authors, Kranz the character, Harris the actor.
candidates.whyNotable: Transcribed exactly on Wikiquote with no dispute note. Pairs instructively with "Failure is not an option" — both are lines given to the Kranz character by the same writers, but only one of them has escaped the film and been pinned on the real man. Useful anchor showing the corpus is not claiming every Kranz-character line is misattributed.

candidates.quote: Lips red as the rose, hair black as ebony, skin white as snow.
candidates.trueOrigin: Spoken by the Slave in the Magic Mirror (voiced by Moroni Olsen), naming Snow White for Queen Grimhilde, in Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937). Shared story credit: Ted Sears, Richard Creedon, Otto Englander, Dick Rickard, Earl Hurd, Merrill De Maris, Dorothy Ann Blank and Webb Smith; Walt Disney Productions (rights holder). ORIGINATION: the imagery is the Brothers Grimm's, not Disney's — the 1812 tale describes the child as white as snow, red as blood, and black as ebony. The film reworks it (rose for blood, and applies it to lips/hair/skin in that order); this specific wording is the film's.
candidates.whyNotable: Second anchor. Useful because it is a case where the film is popularly credited with imagery it inherited from the 1812 Grimm tale and only resharpened — the borrowed-line error class, in a mild form, on a line whose film wording is nonetheless exactly transcribed.

candidates.quote: Lunch is for wimps.
candidates.trueOrigin: Spoken verbatim by Gordon Gekko (Michael Douglas) as part of the transcribed line "Lunch? Aw, you gotta be kidding. Lunch is for wimps." — written by Stanley Weiser and Oliver Stone, Wall Street (1987), 20th Century Fox.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor. The popular short form is an accurate excerpt, not a misquote — the four words are spoken exactly as quoted, with only the preceding sentences dropped. Useful as a contrast case against the two disputed entries on the same title.

candidates.quote: Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?
candidates.trueOrigin: Spoken by Queen Grimhilde (voiced by Lucille La Verne) to the Slave in the Magic Mirror (voiced by Moroni Olsen) in Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937). Shared story credit: Ted Sears, Richard Creedon, Otto Englander, Dick Rickard, Earl Hurd, Merrill De Maris, Dorothy Ann Blank and Webb Smith; supervising director David Hand; Walt Disney Productions (rights holder, work-for-hire). Adapted from the Brothers Grimm tale (1812), whose corresponding line reads "Mirror, mirror on the wall" — the "Magic Mirror" phrasing is the film's own change, not the fairy tale's.
candidates.whyNotable: The film's signature line and the correct-wording anchor for the misquote page above. Transcribed exactly at Wikiquote, and consistent across both of the Queen's invocations. It was on AFI's 400-quote nominating ballot for '100 Years...100 Movie Quotes' but did NOT make the final 100 — do not assert a ranking for it.

candidates.quote: Momma says stupid is as stupid does.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Eric Roth; Forrest Gump (1994), dir. Robert Zemeckis, Paramount Pictures (rights holder). Spoken by young Forrest, answering young Jenny's "Are you stupid or something?" Wikiquote transcribes it only in this prefixed form. ORIGINATION: the construction reworks a much older English proverb, "handsome is as handsome does" (attested from the late 16th–17th century), so the film restated an existing formula rather than coining one — however that proverb link is NOT documented at Wikiquote or Quote Investigator and is flagged for verification rather than asserted.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor, filed deliberately in its transcribed form. The public quotes the bare sentence "Stupid is as stupid does," and Wikiquote shows the line only with the "Momma says" prefix — but see notes: I could not source an absence claim, so I did NOT file this as a misquote. The proverb ancestry is the interesting angle if a researcher can document it at one of our authorities.

candidates.quote: Money never sleeps, pal.
candidates.trueOrigin: Spoken by Gordon Gekko (Michael Douglas): "Money never sleeps, pal. I just made $800,000 in Hong Kong gold." — written by Stanley Weiser and Oliver Stone, Wall Street (1987), 20th Century Fox. The 2010 sequel, Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps, took its title from the line.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor. Transcribed exactly as popularly quoted; the common form merely drops the trailing "pal." The sequel's title cemented the wording, which is why it has not drifted the way the greed line did.

candidates.quote: No! Try not. Do... or do not. There is no try.
candidates.trueOrigin: Star Wars: Episode V — The Empire Strikes Back (1980), screenplay credited to Leigh Brackett & Lawrence Kasdan, story by George Lucas; directed by Irvin Kershner. Lucasfilm Ltd. / Twentieth Century-Fox. Spoken by Yoda (performed and voiced by Frank Oz) on Dagobah, answering Luke's "All right, I'll give it a try." Wikiquote's wikitext transcribes the line as above. The line originated in the film — Empire has no source novel or play; the novelization (Donald F. Glut, 1980) followed the screenplay. Popularly shortened to "Do or do not. There is no try.", which is a truncation rather than a distortion: every quoted word is spoken, only the leading "No! Try not." is dropped. Recorded here as a verified anchor, NOT as a misquote.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-quoted lines in cinema and ubiquitous in management and self-help writing. Valuable as an anchor precisely because it is the near-miss case: the popular short form is a truncation, not a misquote, so it demonstrates where the corpus draws the line between drift and abridgement.

candidates.quote: Now you know why they call me 'Dirty Harry'. I get every dirty job that comes along.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine line, transcribed at Wikiquote. Spoken by Inspector Harry Callahan, played by Clint Eastwood. Dirty Harry (1971), Warner Bros. / The Malpaso Company, directed by Don Siegel. Screenplay credited to Harry Julian Fink, R.M. Fink and Dean Riesner (story by Harry Julian Fink & R.M. Fink), with uncredited contributions from John Milius, Terrence Malick and Jo Heims — the credit is shared and this line is not assigned to any one of them by the sources consulted. Original screenplay, not adapted from a novel or play. Rights holder is the studio (Warner Bros.), not the screenwriters.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor. The line that explains the title and the nickname, quoted exactly as transcribed — useful as a verified counterweight on a title whose two most famous lines are both documented errors.

candidates.quote: People will come, Ray. People will most definitely come.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Phil Alden Robinson, Field of Dreams (1989, Universal Pictures), based on W. P. Kinsella's novel Shoeless Joe (1982). Spoken by the character Terence Mann, played by James Earl Jones. Transcribed exactly at Wikiquote as part of the longer monologue: "The one constant through all the years, Ray, has been baseball... This field, this game; it's a part of our past, Ray. It reminds us of all that once was good, and that could be again. Oh…people will come, Ray. People will most definitely come." ORIGINATION CAVEAT: the film is an adaptation, and the equivalent monologue in the novel is delivered by a fictionalised J. D. Salinger (whom the Terence Mann character replaces). I did NOT establish whether this monologue has a direct antecedent in Kinsella's text, so the Robinson attribution should be treated as the screen credit rather than a settled origination claim — verify against the novel before the page asserts Robinson originated it.
candidates.whyNotable: The film's other signature passage and the likely vector for the "they will come" contamination — Terence Mann says "people will come" plural, minutes of screen time from the singular "he will come", which plausibly explains how the public merged the two. Useful as an anchor and as evidence on the misquote page for HOW the drift happened. Wikiquote transcribes it exactly.

candidates.quote: Round up the usual suspects.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein and Howard Koch — Casablanca (1942), dir. Michael Curtiz, Warner Bros. (work-for-hire; rights holder Warner Bros., not the writers). Spoken by Captain Louis Renault, played by Claude Rains — the actor is the speaker, not the author. Adapted from the unproduced 1940 play "Everybody Comes to Rick's" by Murray Burnett and Joan Alison; Wikiquote does not establish whether the line originated in the play.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor for the title: sourced exactly on Wikiquote and ranked #32 in AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes. Transcribed in context — Renault says "Major Strasser has been shot." then, after a pause, the line — shielding Rick. It entered English as a stock idiom for a token investigation and later titled a 1995 film, so it is heavily searched, and its authorship is routinely credited to Claude Rains or to the film rather than to the writers.

candidates.quote: Run, Forrest! Run!
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Eric Roth; Forrest Gump (1994), dir. Robert Zemeckis, Paramount Pictures (rights holder). Wikiquote transcribes the line exactly as "Run, Forrest! Run!" and gives the speaker as Jenny — shouted when schoolyard bullies chase Forrest — NOT as a Forrest line, though it is widely assumed to be one. Based on Winston Groom's 1986 novel; Wikiquote does not attribute this line to the novel.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor. Wikiquote sources the wording exactly, and the popular rendering differs only in punctuation ("Run, Forrest, run!"), not in words — so this is genuinely said, not a misquote. Its value is as a speaker/writer separation case: the public treats it as Forrest's own catchphrase when Jenny says it, and the author under our house convention is Roth regardless.

candidates.quote: So, eleven hundred men went in the water, three hundred and sixteen men come out, and the sharks took the rest, June the 29th, 1945.
candidates.trueOrigin: Spoken by Quint (Robert Shaw) in Jaws (1975) — the closing lines of the USS Indianapolis monologue; transcribed verbatim at Wikiquote. AUTHORSHIP IS GENUINELY DISPUTED and should be stated as disputed rather than resolved: the credited screenplay is Peter Benchley and Carl Gottlieb, but neither is generally credited with this speech. Howard Sackler, doing an uncredited rewrite, devised the backstory of Quint as an Indianapolis survivor and wrote a 'three-quarters of a page' version; John Milius expanded it into a monologue; Robert Shaw, himself a playwright, then partially rewrote it. Spielberg describes it as a collaboration between Sackler, Milius and Shaw; Carl Gottlieb gives primary credit to Shaw and downplays Milius's contribution. Wikipedia states plainly that 'the question of who deserves the most credit for writing Quint's monologue about the Indianapolis has caused substantial controversy.' ORIGINATION: not from Benchley's 1974 novel — the Indianapolis backstory was created during the film's development (Sackler). Note the speaker/author split: Robert Shaw is both the actor and a partial author here, which is unusual and worth stating explicitly. Rights holder (work-for-hire): Universal Pictures / Zanuck-Brown Company.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor. One of the most celebrated monologues in American cinema and heavily searched. Its value to this corpus is that it is a clean demonstration of the house authorship rule: the line is near-universally attributed to 'Quint' (a character) or to Robert Shaw (an actor), while the credited screenwriters did not write it and the actual writing credit is contested three ways. It also carries a real origination correction — audiences assume it came from Benchley's novel, and it did not. Wikiquote transcribes the full monologue, so the wording claim is safe.

candidates.quote: Space. The final frontier. These are the voyages of the Starship Enterprise. Its five-year mission: To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations. To boldly go where no man has gone before.
candidates.trueOrigin: Opening narration of every Star Trek: The Original Series episode (Desilu Productions for NBC, 1966-69), spoken by William Shatner as Captain Kirk; Wikiquote transcribes it exactly under "Repeated lines". Written in August 1966 by Gene Roddenberry with input from producers John D. F. Black and Bob Justman — a committee text with no single credited author. ORIGINATION NOTE: Star Trek did NOT coin "where no man has gone before". The 1958 White House booklet "Introduction to Outer Space" reads "...the thrust of curiosity that leads men to try to go where no one has gone before"; Samuel A. Peeples proposed the phrase as the title of the second pilot, from which it passed into the narration. Earlier analogues include H. P. Lovecraft's "whither no man had gone before" (The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, written 1927, published 1943) and Camões's "by seas never sailed before" (The Lusiads, 1572). Star Trek sharpened and popularised the phrase; it did not invent it.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor. Wikiquote transcribes the narration exactly, and the wording as popularly quoted matches — so this is genuine. Its value to us is the origination finding underneath it: the most famous clause is borrowed from a 1958 US government booklet, which is precisely the error class the site corrects. Note also the persistent secondary myth that the split infinitive was an accident; the narration is deliberate and Wikiquote's transcription settles the wording ('no man', later 'no one' in TNG).

candidates.quote: There's no place like home.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely spoken in the film by Dorothy Gale (Judy Garland) — but NOT originated by it, and this is the correction the record exists to carry. The line is in the source novel: Dorothy says "There is no place like home." to the Scarecrow in Chapter 4 of L. Frank Baum's The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900). The phrase predates Baum too — it is from John Howard Payne's song "Home! Sweet Home!", written for his 1823 opera Clari, or the Maid of Milan (melody by Henry Bishop); Baum's surrounding "be it ever so beautiful" is a direct play on Payne's "be it ever so humble". MGM scores Bishop's Payne melody under this very scene. Film screenplay by Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson and Edgar Allan Woolf, The Wizard of Oz (1939), Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (rights holder). AFI ranks it #23.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor record, and the batch's origination payload. The wording is exact and triple-sourced (Wikiquote film page, AFI #23), so it is safely 'verified' — the error it corrects is not the words but the CREDIT. The film is routinely named as the origin of a line that is Baum's from 1900 and Payne's from 1823, making it a textbook case of a film credited with a line it borrowed. Note the film's repeated closing chant IS the film's own staging: Baum's Dorothy ends the novel wishing to be taken home to Aunt Em, not chanting this phrase.

candidates.quote: This was no boating accident.
candidates.trueOrigin: Spoken by Matt Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) in Jaws (1975) during the autopsy of Chrissie Watkins's remains. Wikiquote transcribes it exactly as 'This was no boating accident.' and, moments later in the same scene, 'Well, this is not a boating accident! It wasn't any propeller, it wasn't any coral reef, and it wasn't Jack the Ripper! It was a shark.' Screenplay credited to Peter Benchley and Carl Gottlieb, based on Benchley's 1974 novel; Gottlieb was in practice the primary screenwriter during production. Rights holder (work-for-hire): Universal Pictures / Zanuck-Brown Company.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor, and a deliberate near-miss worth recording. The line is widely rendered in the wild as 'This was no boat accident' — a real-looking wording drift of exactly the shape this site corrects. But NO authority documents that drift: it appears in neither the AFI Misquotes section (the line is not on the AFI list at all) nor Wikipedia's List of film misquotes, and Quote Investigator has no Jaws coverage. A Wikiquote search for 'no boat accident' returns nothing. Per the hard rule, it is therefore carried as a verified anchor with the transcribed wording, NOT built as a misquote page. If a downstream pass finds a citation for the 'boat accident' popular form, this record can be promoted to category 'disputed' with the popular wording as the quote.

candidates.quote: When a naked man is chasing a woman through an alley with a butcher knife and a hard-on, I figure he isn't out collecting for the Red Cross.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine line, transcribed at Wikiquote. Spoken by Inspector Harry Callahan, played by Clint Eastwood. Dirty Harry (1971), Warner Bros. / The Malpaso Company, directed by Don Siegel. Screenplay credited to Harry Julian Fink, R.M. Fink and Dean Riesner (story by Harry Julian Fink & R.M. Fink), with uncredited contributions from John Milius, Terrence Malick and Jo Heims — shared credit, not assignable to one writer from the sources consulted. Original screenplay, not adapted from a novel or play. Rights holder is the studio (Warner Bros.), not the screenwriters.
candidates.whyNotable: Anchor. One of the film's most-quoted exchanges and a line people genuinely search for, verified against the Wikiquote transcription rather than the user-submitted listicles that garble it. Crude but real and documented — kept under the skip-only-for-hate/harm policy rather than dropped on taste.

candidates.quote: You've a magnificent brain, Moriarty. I admire it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Written by Edwin Blum and William A. Drake for The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (1939), 20th Century Fox; dir. Alfred L. Werker; partially based on William Gillette's 1899 stage play Sherlock Holmes. Spoken by Basil Rathbone as Sherlock Holmes to George Zucco as Professor Moriarty. Rights holder is the studio (work-for-hire), not the writers. Quoted here as the opening of a longer speech; Wikiquote transcribes the full run.
candidates.whyNotable: The film's signature exchange and its most-quoted line — a genuine, exactly-transcribed anchor for the page. Originates in the 1939 screenplay: it is not from the Conan Doyle canon and not from the Gillette play, which matters because this film's other famous line is inherited rather than original.

candidates.quote: I've always believed the British Open is one of the greatest championships in the world
candidates.trueOrigin: Arnold Palmer, Arnold Palmer: Memories, Stories, and Memorabilia from a Life on and Off the Course (2004), p. 52.
candidates.whyNotable: A cleanly book-sourced Palmer quote credited with reviving American interest in the Open Championship; a documented, verifiable anchor.

candidates.quote: Maybe you'll fail most of the time, but until you've dared to try and have brought off an impossible shot from the rough or from the water, you haven't really tasted the game
candidates.trueOrigin: Arnold Palmer, My Game and Yours (1965), p. 83.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, book-sourced Palmer line on daring the impossible shot — a real anchor to sit alongside the debunked feel-good quotes.

candidates.quote: True heroism is remarkably sober, very undramatic. It is not the urge to surpass all others at whatever cost, but the urge to serve others at whatever cost.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ashe; from his commencement address to Ohio Wesleyan University's class of 1991 (May 12, 1991), confirmed by Quote Investigator.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Ashe's most-quoted genuine lines and a QI-confirmed real anchor, useful as a verified counterpoint to the fakes on the hub.

candidates.quote: We must reach out our hand in friendship both to those who would befriend us and those who would be our enemy.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ashe; from his memoir 'Days of Grace' (1994), p. 186, per Wikiquote's sourced entry.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, sourced Ashe line from his memoir that provides a real anchor alongside the debunked material.

candidates.quote: I was born with an enormous need for affection, and a terrible need to give it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Hepburn, from a New York Times interview (April 22, 1991).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely quoted, genuinely sourced Hepburn line that serves as a real anchor amid the fakes.

candidates.quote: Living is like tearing through a museum. Not until later do you really start absorbing what you saw, thinking about it, looking it up in a book, and remembering — because you can't take it all in at once.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Hepburn, cited in "Audrey Hepburn: A Bio-bibliography" (1994) by David Hofstede.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Hepburn reflection documented in a Wikiquote-cited biography, useful as a verified anchor.

candidates.quote: You just can't beat the person who never gives up.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ruth's; published under his byline in 'Bat It Out!', The Rotarian, July 1940.
candidates.whyNotable: A real, sourced Ruth line and a rare confirmed one: QI verifies Ruth wrote it under his own byline in the article 'Bat It Out!' in The Rotarian, July 1940.

candidates.quote: There's a lot of blood, sweat and guts between dreams and success.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely attributed to Bryant on Wikiquote's sourced 'Quotes' section (cited via Saturday Down South, 2012).
candidates.whyNotable: One of Bryant's most-shared real motivational lines and a solid verified anchor to sit alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: In all my years of football I've never known a man who talked more and won less than Steve Gutman.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bill Belichick, 2000 resignation remarks (reprinted in From Darkness to Dynasty)
candidates.whyNotable: Belichick's famously blunt parting shot at the Jets president when he resigned as 'HC of the NYJ' after one day; a verified, widely reprinted line.

candidates.quote: We're on to Cincinnati.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bill Belichick, New England Patriots press conference, September 29, 2014
candidates.whyNotable: Belichick's most iconic press-conference line, repeated to deflect every question after a 41-14 loss to Kansas City; now shorthand for tuning out noise and moving to the next game.

candidates.quote: A football team is like a piano. You need eight men to carry it and three who can play the damn thing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Shankly, quoted by John Toshack via Kevin McCarra, 'How Benitez built Liverpool,' The Guardian (21 Jan 2006).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-quoted Shankly aphorism on team roles, sourced at Wikiquote to a Guardian recollection by John Toshack.

candidates.quote: At a football club, there's a holy trinity - the players, the manager and the supporters.
candidates.trueOrigin: Shankly, cited in 'Bill Shankly: Life, death and football,' The Guardian (18 Oct 2009).
candidates.whyNotable: A defining statement of Shankly's fan-first football philosophy, sourced at Wikiquote to a Guardian retrospective.

candidates.quote: Football is not a matter of life and death. It's much more important than that.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Shankly, but the popular meme wording is a tidied paraphrase. In a 1981 Granada TV interview he actually said: 'Someone said to me To you football is a matter of life or death! and I said Listen, it's more important than that.'
candidates.whyNotable: Shankly's most-shared line, endlessly repeated in this polished form; the real 1981 TV wording documented by Wikiquote is looser and was said with regret, not bravado.

candidates.quote: The socialism I believe in is everyone working for each other, everyone having a share of the rewards. It's the way I see football, the way I see life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Shankly, documented in Powley & Gillan, 'Shankly's Village' (Pitch, 2015).
candidates.whyNotable: Shankly's much-quoted articulation of football-as-socialism; sourced at Wikiquote to a 2015 biography of his home village of Glenbuck.

candidates.quote: Pressure is a privilege.
candidates.trueOrigin: Billie Jean King, title of her 2008 book Pressure Is a Privilege
candidates.whyNotable: Genuinely King's signature phrase and the title of her 2008 book.

candidates.quote: Crazy-busy is a great armor, it's a great way for numbing. What a lot of us do is that we stay so busy, and so out in front of our life, that the truth of how we're feeling and what we really need can't catch up with us.
candidates.trueOrigin: Brené Brown, Washington Post interview, October 2012 (as cited on Wikiquote).
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently excerpted 'crazy-busy as armor' line; sourced on Wikiquote to an October 2012 Washington Post interview, giving the Brown hub a verifiable anchor.

candidates.quote: Shame hates to have words wrapped around it. If we talk about it, it loses its grip on us.
candidates.trueOrigin: Brené Brown, University of Houston 'Pride Stories' (as cited on Wikiquote).
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared as the core of Brown's shame-resilience message ('shame derives its power from being unspeakable'); sourced on Wikiquote to a University of Houston Pride Stories piece.

candidates.quote: Vulnerability is not weakness; it's our greatest measure of courage.
candidates.trueOrigin: Brené Brown, Atlas of the Heart: Mapping Meaningful Connection and the Language of Human Experience (2021).
candidates.whyNotable: One of Brown's signature lines and the thesis of her whole body of work on vulnerability; sourced on Wikiquote to her 2021 book Atlas of the Heart.

candidates.quote: A teacher, a really good sensei, is never a giver of 'truth'; he is a guide, a pointer to the truth that the student must discover for himself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bruce Lee, 'Liberate Yourself from Classical Karate,' Black Belt magazine, September 1971
candidates.whyNotable: A rare case where the popular attribution holds up: QI confirms Bruce Lee wrote it in his essay 'Liberate Yourself from Classical Karate' in the September 1971 Black Belt magazine, making it a strong verified anchor amid his many fakes.

candidates.quote: Be water, my friend.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bruce Lee, 1971 Pierre Berton interview; documented in Bruce Lee: A Warrior's Journey (2000)
candidates.whyNotable: Bruce Lee's signature line, from his 1971 Pierre Berton television interview and preserved in Bruce Lee: A Warrior's Journey (2000) — the real, sourced anchor the internet's fakes cluster around.

candidates.quote: Don't think. Feel. It is like a finger pointing away to the moon. Don't concentrate on the finger or you will miss all that heavenly glory.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bruce Lee's character in the film Enter the Dragon (1973)
candidates.whyNotable: One of Bruce Lee's most-quoted movie lines, spoken by his character in Enter the Dragon (1973) and sourced on Wikiquote — genuinely from the film even though it is often shortened and reworded online.

candidates.quote: Friendship is born at that moment when one person says to another, 'What! You too? I thought I was the only one.'
candidates.trueOrigin: C.S. Lewis, The Four Loves (1960).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced and beloved Lewis line on friendship, a strong verified anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: There are two kinds of people in the end: those who say to God, 'Thy will be done,' and those to whom God says, 'Thy will be done.'
candidates.trueOrigin: C.S. Lewis, The Great Divorce (1945).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, widely quoted Lewis line with a documented source, useful as a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: The meeting of two personalities is like the contact of two chemical substances: if there is any reaction, both are transformed.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Jung: Modern Man in Search of a Soul (1933), p. 49.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Jung's most-quoted verified lines with a solid Wikiquote source; a real anchor for the provenance hub.

candidates.quote: Can't anybody here play this game?
candidates.trueOrigin: Casey Stengel, on the hapless 1962 New York Mets; used as the title of Jimmy Breslin's 1963 book
candidates.whyNotable: Stengel's signature lament over the expansion Mets and one of baseball's most-quoted lines, verified via Breslin's 1963 book title.

candidates.quote: I'll never make the mistake of being 70 years old again
candidates.trueOrigin: Casey Stengel, on being fired by the Yankees after the 1960 World Series (quoted in Joseph Durso's 1967 biography)
candidates.whyNotable: Stengel's famous quip on his forced retirement from the Yankees, sourced in his 1967 biography.

candidates.quote: The secret of managing is to keep the guys who hate you away from the ones who are undecided
candidates.trueOrigin: Casey Stengel, popular condensation of a longer remark at the December 1964 Winter Meetings (recalled by Bob Sudyk, Hartford Courant, 1993)
candidates.whyNotable: One of Stengel's most-repeated management aphorisms; the pithy popular wording is a condensation of a longer sourced 1964 remark on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: There comes a time in every man's life, and I've had plenty of them
candidates.trueOrigin: Casey Stengel, quoted in Parade magazine, August 23, 1953
candidates.whyNotable: A quintessential piece of self-aware 'Stengelese', sourced to a 1953 Parade profile.

candidates.quote: Without losers, where would the winners be?
candidates.trueOrigin: Casey Stengel, quoted in The Gospel According to Casey (1992), ed. Berkow & Kaplan, p. 19
candidates.whyNotable: A characteristic Stengel one-liner on competition, sourced to the 1992 anthology of his sayings.

candidates.quote: An intellectual is a man who says a simple thing in a difficult way; an artist is a man who says a difficult thing in a simple way.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Bukowski, Notes of a Dirty Old Man (1969).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, frequently-quoted Bukowski aphorism with a real source citation on Wikiquote (Notes of a Dirty Old Man, 1969), giving the hub a verified anchor.

candidates.quote: The free soul is rare, but you know it when you see it — basically because you feel good, very good, when you are near or with them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Bukowski, Tales of Ordinary Madness.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine and heavily-circulated Bukowski line sourced on Wikiquote to Tales of Ordinary Madness, useful as a verified real anchor among the misattributions.

candidates.quote: We are here to laugh at the odds and live our lives so well that Death will tremble to take us.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Bukowski, Life Magazine (December 1988), 'The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture'.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, widely-shared Bukowski line with a solid citation — part of his answer in Life Magazine's December 1988 'The Meaning of Life' feature — making it a strong real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Fashion fades, only style remains the same.
candidates.trueOrigin: Coco Chanel articulated it in a 1965 McCall's interview; the underlying idea predates her (an anonymous beauty expert wrote 'Fashion comes and goes, style goes on forever' in 1929).
candidates.whyNotable: Chanel's single most-quoted line; QI credits her 1965 McCall's articulation ('Fashion passes, style remains') while noting the fashion-vs-style idea circulated as early as 1929, so it is a real Chanel line built on a pre-existing concept.

candidates.quote: Fashion is always a reflection of the times, but it is forgotten if it is foolish.
candidates.trueOrigin: Coco Chanel, 'Maximes et Sentences,' Paris Vogue, September 1938.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Chanel maxim from her September 1938 Paris Vogue 'Maximes et Sentences,' which QI presents as authentically hers rather than disputed.

candidates.quote: Fashion is architecture. It is a matter of proportions.
candidates.trueOrigin: Coco Chanel, via Marcel Haedrich's 1971 biography 'Coco Chanel Secrète.'
candidates.whyNotable: A signature Chanel design maxim on Wikiquote; QI concludes Chanel deserves credit based on her biographer Marcel Haedrich's testimony.

candidates.quote: Nothing is ugly as long as it is alive.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Coco Chanel through Marcel Haedrich's 1971 biography 'Coco Chanel Secrète.'
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently shared Chanel aphorism that QI credits to her, though only via her authorized 1971 biography, so it rests on a single posthumous source.

candidates.quote: Where should one use perfume? Wherever one wants to be kissed.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI credits Coco Chanel; earliest citation a 1962 Boston Globe column, corroborated by Marcel Haedrich's 1971 biography 'Coco Chanel Secrète.'
candidates.whyNotable: One of Chanel's most-quoted witticisms; QI believes she deserves credit, citing a 1962 Boston Globe column and her 1971 authorized biography, though the earliest source is decades after she supposedly said it.

candidates.quote: If you want others to be happy, practice compassion. If you want to be happy, practice compassion.
candidates.trueOrigin: The Dalai Lama, quoted in 'Meditations for Living In Balance' (2000).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, heavily shared compassion line with a sourced Wikiquote entry (Meditations for Living In Balance, 2000) — a real anchor to sit beside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Love and compassion are necessities, not luxuries. Without them humanity cannot survive.
candidates.trueOrigin: The Dalai Lama, 'The Art of Happiness' / compassion writings (cited via A Small Drop of Ink, 2003).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, frequently cited line with a sourced Wikiquote entry, useful as a verified hub anchor alongside the misattributions.

candidates.quote: My true religion is Kindness.
candidates.trueOrigin: The Dalai Lama, 'Kindness, Clarity, and Insight' (1984).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, widely quoted anchor line with a sourced Wikiquote entry from his book Kindness, Clarity, and Insight (1984).

candidates.quote: A person's a person, no matter how small.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely from Dr. Seuss, 'Horton Hears a Who!' (1954).
candidates.whyNotable: A real, book-sourced Seuss line that anchors the hub alongside the debunks; from Horton Hears a Who! (1954).

candidates.quote: The more that you read, the more things you will know. The more that you learn, the more places you'll go.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely from Dr. Seuss, 'I Can Read With My Eyes Shut!' (1978).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, book-sourced Seuss literacy line that serves as a verified anchor; from I Can Read With My Eyes Shut! (1978).

candidates.quote: Do what you feel in your heart to be right, for you'll be criticized anyway.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Eleanor Roosevelt in Dale Carnegie's How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1944); credibly hers but not traced to a first-person source document.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely shared Roosevelt line with a real documentary trail, credited to her in Dale Carnegie's How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1944).

candidates.quote: It takes courage to love, but pain through love is the purifying fire which those who love generously know.
candidates.trueOrigin: Eleanor Roosevelt, My Day column, April 1, 1939.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Roosevelt line, cited by Wikiquote to her My Day newspaper column of April 1, 1939.

candidates.quote: You gain strength, courage, and confidence by every experience in which you really stop to look fear in the face.
candidates.trueOrigin: Eleanor Roosevelt, You Learn by Living (1960), pp. 29-30.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely Roosevelt line, sourced by Wikiquote to her 1960 book You Learn by Living, serving as a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Always look for the helpers. There's always someone who is trying to help.
candidates.trueOrigin: Fred Rogers, 'Mister Rogers Talks with Parents' (Berkley Books, 1983), p. 177
candidates.whyNotable: Rogers' single most-quoted line, recirculated after every disaster; genuinely his, sourced to 'Mister Rogers Talks with Parents' (1983) and 'You Are Special' (1995) on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: As human beings, our job in life is to help people realize how rare and valuable each one of us really is.
candidates.trueOrigin: Fred Rogers, 'Mister Rogers' Neighborhood: Thoughts For All Ages'
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently-shared, genuinely-Rogers line documented on Wikiquote (Mister Rogers' Neighborhood: Thoughts For All Ages) — a real anchor to sit alongside the debunks on a Rogers hub.

candidates.quote: You've made this day a special day, by just your being you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Fred Rogers, U.S. Senate subcommittee testimony, May 1, 1969
candidates.whyNotable: Rogers' signature spoken sign-off, delivered in his famous May 1, 1969 U.S. Senate testimony; genuine and sourced on Wikiquote (song-lyric tail deliberately trimmed).

candidates.quote: All art is propaganda.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Orwell: from his essay 'Charles Dickens' (1940), where he wrote 'All art is propaganda. On the other hand, not all propaganda is art.'
candidates.whyNotable: A real Orwell line QI confirms to his 1940 Dickens essay; verified anchor whose fuller context is often dropped.

candidates.quote: Every joke is a tiny revolution.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Orwell: from his 1945 essay 'Funny, But Not Vulgar' ('A thing is funny when — in some way that is not actually offensive or frightening — it upsets the established order. Every joke is a tiny revolution.').
candidates.whyNotable: A real, quotable Orwell line QI confirms to his 1945 essay on humor; good verified anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: If liberty means anything at all, it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Orwell: from the essay 'The Freedom of the Press', his intended (then unpublished) preface to Animal Farm, 1945.
candidates.whyNotable: A real, well-sourced Orwell line and a strong verified anchor for the hub; QI confirms the Animal Farm preface source.

candidates.quote: It's hard not to play golf that's up to Jack Nicklaus standards when you are Jack Nicklaus.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jack Nicklaus
candidates.whyNotable: A rare sourced Nicklaus line on Wikiquote, said on WINS Radio after winning his 70th PGA tournament, useful as a verified anchor alongside debunks.

candidates.quote: The older you get the stronger the wind gets - and it's always in your face.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jack Nicklaus
candidates.whyNotable: One of the two quotes Wikiquote actually sources to Nicklaus (International Herald Tribune, 28 Feb 1990); a widely-shared, verifiable anchor line.

candidates.quote: A life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jackie Robinson, I Never Had It Made (as told to Alfred Duckett), 1972
candidates.whyNotable: Robinson's single most-shared line and the epitaph on his gravestone; a genuine, well-sourced anchor worth a page as a verified hub for this magnet author.

candidates.quote: I cannot stand and sing the anthem. I cannot salute the flag. I know that I am a black man in a white world.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jackie Robinson, I Never Had It Made (as told to Alfred Duckett), 1972
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently doubted or challenged online as too pointed to be real, yet it is genuinely sourced to his 1972 autobiography - high fact-check value for a 'did he really say this?' page.

candidates.quote: I'm not concerned with your liking or disliking me. All I ask is that you respect me as a human being.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jackie Robinson, response to an umpire c.1954; quoted in Baseball Has Done It (1964), pp. 9-10
candidates.whyNotable: One of Robinson's most-quoted lines on dignity and respect; Wikiquote sources it firmly to Baseball Has Done It (1964), making it a strong verified anchor.

candidates.quote: Find the good. It's all around you. Find it, showcase it and you'll start believing in it.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently doubted as too pat to be real, but Quote Investigator CONFIRMS it — traced to Owens's 1970 Blackthink, ch. 8 'Showcase the Good,' via scans of the original.

candidates.quote: Hitler didn't snub me; it was our president who snubbed me. The president didn't even send me a telegram.
candidates.whyNotable: Owens's own words debunking the ubiquitous 'Hitler snubbed Owens at the 1936 Olympics' myth; documented in Jeremy Schaap's Triumph (2007) and on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: I had four gold medals, but you can't eat four gold medals.
candidates.whyNotable: Iconic Owens line about racing horses for money after 1936; verified from a 1971 interview cited by ESPN SportsCentury and Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: The battles that count aren't the ones for gold medals. The struggles within yourself — the invisible, inevitable battles inside all of us — that's where it's at.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared inspirational Owens lines online; genuinely his, from his 1970 book Blackthink, and a strong real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: The road to the Olympics, leads to no city, no country. It goes far beyond New York or Moscow, ancient Greece or Nazi Germany. The road to the Olympics leads — in the end — to the best within us.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely circulated Owens Olympic quote; verified via Voice of America's People In America (2002) and reproduced on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: We must all suffer from one of two pains: the pain of discipline or the pain of regret. The difference is discipline weighs ounces while regret weighs tons.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Jim Rohn (American motivational speaker, 1930-2009); listed in the main Quotes section of his Wikiquote page, though without a precise book/seminar citation.
candidates.whyNotable: The lone quote featured on Jim Rohn's Wikiquote page and one of his signature motivational lines, widely circulated as a real Rohn aphorism.

candidates.quote: Don't give up. Don't ever give up.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jim Valvano, Arthur Ashe Courage Award speech, first ESPY Awards, March 4, 1993
candidates.whyNotable: Valvano's rallying cry from his 1993 ESPY speech two months before he died of cancer; it became the motto of the V Foundation.

candidates.quote: To me, there are three things everyone should do every day. Number one is laugh. Number two is think. And number three, you should have your emotions moved to tears.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jim Valvano, 1993 ESPY Awards speech
candidates.whyNotable: The 'laugh, think, cry' passage is the emotional core of Valvano's 1993 ESPY speech.

candidates.quote: Make each day your masterpiece.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely a Wooden signature line; he credited the lesson to his father and repeated it throughout his life (e.g. Charlie Rose interview, 2000).
candidates.whyNotable: One of Wooden's best-known and genuinely-his maxims, closely tied to his teaching identity.

candidates.quote: Success is peace of mind which is a direct result of self-satisfaction in knowing you made the effort to become the best of which you are capable.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Wooden — his own definition of success, foundational to his Pyramid of Success; stated in his Charlie Rose interview (2000) and his writings.
candidates.whyNotable: Wooden's single most important and genuinely-authored idea, the definition of success he built his whole philosophy on — a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Talent is God-given; be humble. Fame is man-given; be thankful. Conceit is self-given; be careful.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Wooden, sourced to his 1972 memoir 'They Call Me Coach'.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-shared and genuinely-sourced Wooden line, useful as a verified anchor in the hub.

candidates.quote: The main ingredient of stardom is the rest of the team.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Wooden, sourced to his 1972 memoir 'They Call Me Coach'.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, sourced Wooden line on teamwork that anchors the hub against the misattributed material.

candidates.quote: Get over yourself! 'Cause it's not about you, man.
candidates.trueOrigin: Kobe Bryant, interview with Patrick Bet-David, August 23, 2019 (YouTube).
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, dated interview line that Wikiquote sources precisely — a clean genuine anchor with an exact primary citation.

candidates.quote: I can't believe how fast 20 years went by... Mamba Out!
candidates.trueOrigin: Kobe Bryant, speech after his final game, April 13, 2016.
candidates.whyNotable: The iconic sign-off from Bryant's speech after his final NBA game, one of the most-quoted lines of his career and a real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: No matter what, people are going to like you or not like you. So be authentic, and let them like you or not for who you actually are.
candidates.trueOrigin: Kobe Bryant, The Mamba Mentality: How I Play (2018), 'Keep It Real.'
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, book-sourced Mamba Mentality line that is widely shared and gives the hub a real, citable anchor alongside the disputed material.

candidates.quote: The mamba mentality is a constant quest to try to be better today than you were yesterday.
candidates.trueOrigin: Kobe Bryant, in his own words describing Mamba Mentality
candidates.whyNotable: Kobe's own verbatim definition of Mamba Mentality (as opposed to the many paraphrases), the anchor quote for the concept he created.

candidates.quote: I can think of no more stirring symbol of man's humanity to man than a fire engine.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Vonnegut — dialogue spoken by the character Winston Niles Rumfoord in the 1959 novel The Sirens of Titan; Vonnegut echoed it himself in 2001.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently doubted as a real Vonnegut line, but QI confirms he wrote it in The Sirens of Titan — a verified quote whose provenance people question.

candidates.quote: Please accept our apologies. We were roaring drunk on petroleum.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Vonnegut — his message to future generations delivered at the Connecticut Forum in Hartford in February 2006.
candidates.whyNotable: A biting climate-era line QI confirms Vonnegut actually said at a 2006 public forum — a verified quote with a specific documented occasion.

candidates.quote: So it goes.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Vonnegut — the recurring refrain in Slaughterhouse-Five (1969), spoken after every mention of death.
candidates.whyNotable: Vonnegut's signature verified catchphrase, endlessly quoted — a strong real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: The arts are not a way to make a living. They are a very human way of making life more bearable.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Vonnegut — from his 2005 essay collection A Man Without a Country.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely shared inspirational line that QI confirms is authentically Vonnegut, sourced to A Man Without a Country.

candidates.quote: We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful about what we pretend to be.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Vonnegut — from the introduction to his 1961 novel Mother Night.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Vonnegut's most-quoted real lines and a good verified anchor to sit alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: So I close in saying that I might have been given a bad break, but I've got an awful lot to live for
candidates.trueOrigin: Lou Gehrig, closing line of his July 4, 1939 farewell speech at Yankee Stadium
candidates.whyNotable: The genuine closing line of Gehrig's 1939 farewell address, sourced on Wikiquote; frequently truncated, paraphrased, or blended with the movie script in circulation, so a verified-wording page has real value.

candidates.quote: Today I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth
candidates.trueOrigin: Lou Gehrig, Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day, Yankee Stadium, July 4, 1939 (his farewell speech)
candidates.whyNotable: The most famous line in American sports oratory and a real anchor for the hub; genuinely Gehrig's, but the popular memory of it is disputed — Wikiquote's exact wording is 'Yet today, I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth,' the line actually OPENED the speech rather than closing it, the Pride of the Yankees (1942) film moved it to the climax, and no complete recording survives, so most people 'remember' the Hollywood version.

candidates.quote: He had shoulder surgery on his elbow.
candidates.trueOrigin: Lou Holtz (credibly credited; Wikiquote lists it as Attributed via Bleacher Report without a firm primary source).

candidates.quote: On this team, we're all united in a common goal: to keep my job.

candidates.trueOrigin: Marilyn Monroe, quoted in Ms. magazine, August 1972, p. 40.

candidates.whyNotable: QI credits King with this formulation (used ~1954-55, published 1964), though earlier thematic precursors existed; a verified anchor line.

candidates.quote: I did then what I knew how to do. Now that I know better, I do better.
candidates.trueOrigin: Maya Angelou, credited by Oprah Winfrey and documented in a 1995 Washington Post article.

candidates.trueOrigin: Maya Angelou, 1988 PBS documentary Facing Evil (Bill Moyers).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Angelou statement QI traces to the March 28, 1988 PBS/Bill Moyers documentary Facing Evil; later reference works corrupted 'tragic' to 'pitiful'.

candidates.quote: Without courage, you can't practice any other virtue consistently.
candidates.trueOrigin: Maya Angelou, quoted in USA Today, March 5, 1988.

candidates.quote: You may encounter many defeats, but you must not be defeated.

candidates.quote: Never say never, because limits, like fears, are often just an illusion.
candidates.trueOrigin: Michael Jordan, Basketball Hall of Fame induction speech, September 11, 2009

candidates.quote: Everybody has plans until they get hit for the first time.

candidates.quote: I probably have a 20,000-word vocabulary. I'll match my wits with anyone on literature, science and the arts.

candidates.quote: These books ain't window dressing. I think Machiavelli's the most sophisticated writer outside of Shakespeare.

candidates.whyNotable: Often-shared 'Tyson on literature' line that surprises people; sourced on Wikiquote to the Telegraph.

candidates.quote: Don't look for big things, just do small things with great love. The smaller the thing, the greater must be our love.

candidates.quote: The biggest disease today is not leprosy or tuberculosis, but rather the feeling of being unwanted.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mother Teresa, quoted in Malcolm Muggeridge, 'Something Beautiful for God' (1971).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Mother Teresa line that anchors the hub; Wikiquote cites it to Malcolm Muggeridge's 'Something Beautiful for God' (1971).

candidates.quote: He who is not courageous enough to take risks will accomplish nothing in life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ali; earliest documented instance is an April 1977 Fort Lauderdale News report, and he reused it through 1980. QI credits Ali.
candidates.whyNotable: Often shared as generic inspiration but genuinely Ali's; QI confirms he coined it, using it repeatedly from April 1977 and even asking a reporter to write it down.

candidates.quote: I am the greatest! I'm the greatest thing that ever lived.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ali; spoken after defeating Sonny Liston, February 25, 1964, as documented on Wikiquote.
candidates.whyNotable: Ali's defining self-declaration, shouted after upsetting Sonny Liston on February 25, 1964; a genuine sourced anchor line.

candidates.quote: I'm so fast last night I cut the light switch and was in bed before the room was dark.
candidates.trueOrigin: Ali delivered this version (recorded by a Village Voice reporter in 1974); QI notes the underlying 'in bed before the room was dark' joke circulated earlier, so Ali adapted an existing gag.
candidates.whyNotable: A classic Ali speed boast that is genuinely his; QI traces the wording to a 1974 Village Voice report, while noting the joke form predates him.

candidates.quote: My conscience won't let me go shoot my brother, or some darker people, or some poor hungry people in the mud, for big powerful America
candidates.trueOrigin: Muhammad Ali, 1967, on refusing induction into the U.S. military
candidates.whyNotable: Ali's genuine, Wikiquote-sourced 1967 explanation for refusing Vietnam draft induction - a historically documented real quote to anchor the hub.

candidates.quote: The man who views the world at 50 the same as he did at 20 has wasted 30 years of his life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Ali; delivered at a November 1974 London news conference (reported by UPI) and repeated in a November 1975 Playboy interview.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely quoted Ali reflection that is actually genuine; QI confirms Ali said it at a 1974 London news conference, with a concise version in a 1975 Playboy interview.

candidates.quote: No one is born hating another person because of the colour of his skin, or his background, or his religion. People must learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Mandela; from his 1994 autobiography Long Walk to Freedom.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, widely-shared Mandela passage with a clear book source; strong genuine anchor alongside the misattribution debunks.

candidates.quote: Be alone, that is the secret of invention; be alone, that is when ideas are born.
candidates.trueOrigin: Nikola Tesla, New York Times interview, April 8, 1934.
candidates.whyNotable: A heavily shared creativity quote that QI confirmed is authentic, from Tesla's April 8, 1934 New York Times interview with Orrin E. Dunlap Jr.

candidates.quote: The scientific man does not aim at an immediate result. His duty is to lay the foundation for those who are to come, and point the way.
candidates.trueOrigin: Nikola Tesla, Modern Mechanics and Inventions, July 1934.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Tesla line on the purpose of science; Wikiquote cites Modern Mechanics and Inventions, July 1934, providing a verified anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Computers are useless. They can only give you answers.
candidates.trueOrigin: Traces to a 1964 Paris Review interview by William Fifield, where Picasso said of calculating machines 'But they are useless. They can only give you answers.' The modern 'computers' wording was refined over 1967-1986.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Picasso's most-quoted lines that QI actually substantiates, sourcing it to a documented 1964 Paris Review interview even though the 'computers' wording was polished later.

candidates.quote: There is only one thing that makes a dream impossible to achieve: the fear of failure.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paulo Coelho, The Alchemist (1988), p. 141
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced and heavily shared Alchemist line (1988), useful as a verified anchor alongside the misattributions.

candidates.quote: Warriors of the light are not perfect. Their beauty lies in accepting this fact and still desiring to grow and to learn.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paulo Coelho, Manual of the Warrior of Light (1997)
candidates.whyNotable: A real, Wikiquote-sourced line from Manual of the Warrior of Light (1997), giving the hub a second genuine anchor beyond The Alchemist.

candidates.quote: When you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paulo Coelho, The Alchemist (1988), p. 22
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line from The Alchemist and a real, sourced Coelho quote (p. 22 of the 1988 novel) that anchors the hub against the debunks.

candidates.quote: Every kid around the world who plays soccer wants to be Pelé. I have a great responsibility to show them not just how to be like a soccer player, but how to be like a man.
candidates.trueOrigin: Pelé — as quoted in Sports Illustrated (1 June 1999).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, sourced Pelé quote and a strong real anchor for a hub — cited on Wikiquote to Sports Illustrated's 1999 'SI Flashback: Soccer's greatest genius.'

candidates.quote: I was born for soccer, just as Beethoven was born for music.
candidates.trueOrigin: Pelé — quoted in Parton Keese, The Measure of Greatness (1980).
candidates.whyNotable: A famous, sourced Pelé line — Wikiquote cites it to Parton Keese, 'The Measure of Greatness' (1980); a clean verified anchor.

candidates.quote: Efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, 'Managing for Business Effectiveness,' Harvard Business Review (1963).
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-quoted management aphorisms whose attribution is often doubted online; QI confirms Drucker articulated it in his 1963 HBR article.

candidates.quote: Strong people always have strong weaknesses too
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, The Effective Executive (1967).
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently-shared leadership line; QI confirms Drucker wrote it in his 1967 book The Effective Executive.

candidates.quote: Success always obsoletes the very behavior that achieved it
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973), p. 88.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely-sourced Drucker insight on success and change with a cited Wikiquote entry, useful as a verified anchor.

candidates.quote: The purpose of an organization is to enable common men to do uncommon things
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973), p. 455.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-shared, genuinely-sourced Drucker line on organizations; strong verified anchor with a cited Wikiquote entry.

candidates.quote: There is only one valid definition of a business purpose: to create a customer
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, The Practice of Management (1954), p. 37.
candidates.whyNotable: A cornerstone Drucker management dictum with a sourced Wikiquote entry, useful as a verified anchor.

candidates.quote: There is surely nothing quite so useless as doing with great efficiency what should not be done at all
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, 'Managing for Business Effectiveness,' Harvard Business Review (1963).
candidates.whyNotable: Widely cited and sometimes questioned; QI confirms Drucker coined this exact wording in his 1963 HBR article, though earlier thematically similar remarks exist.

candidates.quote: Thirty years from now the big university campuses will be relics
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, interview published in Forbes (1997).
candidates.whyNotable: A famous and often-recirculated Drucker prediction; QI confirms he said it in a 1997 Forbes interview.

candidates.quote: When a subject becomes totally obsolete we make it a required course
candidates.trueOrigin: Peter Drucker, who used variant phrasings across 1969, 1976, and 1992 works.
candidates.whyNotable: A popular jab at academia; QI credits Drucker, who circulated the idea in multiple works from 1969 onward.

candidates.quote: You handle animals. You deal with people.
candidates.trueOrigin: Red Auerbach; sourced in Billy Packer & Roland Lazenby, Why We Win (Masters Press, 1999), p. 15.
candidates.whyNotable: Auerbach's genuinely-sourced signature line on his people-first coaching philosophy — the one quote Wikiquote documents with a citation, useful as a real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: Death is nature's way of saying, 'Your table is ready.'
candidates.trueOrigin: Credited to Robin Williams via Wikiquote (citing The Fourth...637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said, 1990); as a compact one-liner its ultimate origin is not fully pinned.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous gallows-humor line credited to Williams and sourced on Wikiquote, though the compact joke format means the exact origin is not ironclad — worth an anchor page with a light provenance caveat.

candidates.quote: I wonder what chairs think about all day: 'Oh, here comes another asshole.'
candidates.trueOrigin: Robin Williams, Reality...What a Concept (1979), per Wikiquote.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-circulated genuine Williams stand-up bit, sourced on Wikiquote to his 1979 special Reality...What a Concept — a verified anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: You're only given a little spark of madness. You mustn't lose it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Robin Williams, early stand-up / A Night at the Roxy era (late 1970s), as sourced on Wikiquote.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Williams' most-shared genuine lines about creativity, from his early stand-up and sourced on Wikiquote — a real anchor to sit alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Cool Papa was so fast that he could turn off the light switch and get into bed before the room got dark.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paige's tribute to teammate Cool Papa Bell; QI dates his use of the expression to 1969 (also recorded in The Washington Post, April 29, 1969).
candidates.whyNotable: A famous, verified Negro Leagues one-liner genuinely from Paige, giving the hub a real anchor with a clean 1969 citation.

candidates.quote: Don't look back. Something might be gaining on you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paige's — published in the sidebar 'How to Stay Young' of Richard Donovan's June 13, 1953 Collier's profile 'Time Ain't Gonna Mess with Me.' QI concludes Paige deserves credit.
candidates.whyNotable: Paige's single most iconic line and a verified anchor; QI credits it to Paige via the 1953 Collier's 'How to Stay Young' feature.

candidates.quote: I have never thrown an illegal pitch. The trouble is some of my pitches were never seen by this generation until I came along.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Paige's — QI's earliest citation is the March 5, 1958 Miami Herald ('Psychiatrist Satch Set for Season'); Paige delivered it repeatedly with varying wording.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, widely-quoted Paige wisecrack with a solid 1958 source, useful as a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: One day, in retrospect, the years of struggle will strike you as the most beautiful.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine Freud, 1907 letter to C. G. Jung; popular English wording from the 1960 Letters of Sigmund Freud translation.
candidates.whyNotable: A rare inspirational line correctly credited to Freud; QI verified it via scans of his September 19, 1907 letter to C. G. Jung.

candidates.quote: The great question that has never been answered, and which I have not yet been able to answer, despite my thirty years of research into the feminine soul, is 'What does a woman want?'
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine Freud, reported by Marie Bonaparte and quoted in Ernest Jones's biography (1953).
candidates.whyNotable: Freud's famous 'What does a woman want?' remark, documented via Marie Bonaparte's record (as cited by Ernest Jones) rather than a published Freud work.

candidates.quote: Real artists ship.
candidates.trueOrigin: Quote Investigator concludes Jobs both coined and popularized it, per Andy Hertzfeld's account of a January 1983 Macintosh team offsite ('Quotations from Chairman Jobs').
candidates.whyNotable: A rare case where the popular attribution holds — QI confirms Jobs likely originated this Silicon Valley mantra, making it a strong verified anchor.

candidates.quote: Your time is limited, so don't waste it living someone else's life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely said by Jobs in his Stanford University commencement address, June 12, 2005.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Jobs's most-quoted real lines, with a firm primary source, giving the hub a verified anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: A man has to have goals — for a day, for a lifetime — and that was mine, to have people say, 'There goes Ted Williams, the greatest hitter who ever lived.'
candidates.whyNotable: Williams' signature life ambition, primary-sourced to his autobiography My Turn at Bat (1970) — a real anchor amid the fakes and his single most-quoted line.

candidates.quote: If you don't think too good, don't think too much.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous Williams witticism carried on the main Wikiquote page, though sourced only to a 2007 quotations compendium rather than a primary record, so its exact provenance is soft.

candidates.quote: A real decision is measured by the fact that you've taken a new action
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Robbins — Awaken the Giant Within (1992), p. 49.
candidates.whyNotable: Signature Robbins line on decision-making, sourced by Wikiquote to Awaken the Giant Within (1992).

candidates.quote: All personal breakthroughs begin with a change in beliefs
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Robbins — Awaken the Giant Within (1992), p. 85.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently reshared genuine Robbins line, sourced by Wikiquote to Awaken the Giant Within (1992).

candidates.quote: Beliefs have the power to create and the power to destroy
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Robbins — Awaken the Giant Within (1992), p. 75.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared genuine Robbins line, sourced by Wikiquote to Awaken the Giant Within (1992).

candidates.quote: The quality of your life is the quality of your communication
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Robbins — Unlimited Power (1986), p. 198.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Robbins' most-quoted genuine lines, sourced by Wikiquote to his 1986 book Unlimited Power; a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: I only hope that we never lose sight of one thing — that it was all started by a mouse.

candidates.quote: We keep moving forward, opening new doors, and doing new things, because we're curious and curiosity keeps leading us down new paths.
candidates.trueOrigin: Walt Disney, as quoted in the ending credits of Meet the Robinsons (2007).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-shared Disney quote with a real documented source in the closing credits of Meet the Robinsons.

candidates.quote: In a world of individuals, comparison is a senseless activity.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Wayne Dyer — sourced by Wikiquote to his 1978 book Pulling Your Own Strings.
candidates.whyNotable: A real, book-sourced Dyer line (Pulling Your Own Strings, 1978) that serves as a verified anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: You will never win if you have to prove that you are the winner.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Wayne Dyer — sourced by Wikiquote to his 1978 book Pulling Your Own Strings.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, Wikiquote-sourced Dyer line from Pulling Your Own Strings (1978), a real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: You miss 100% of the shots you don't take.

candidates.quote: I really didn't say everything I said.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Yogi Berra; title/text of The Yogi Book (1997)
candidates.whyNotable: The perfect anchor for a misattribution hub: a verified Berra line (title of The Yogi Book, 1997) in which he himself acknowledges the pile of quotes wrongly credited to him.

candidates.quote: It ain't over till it's over.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Yogi Berra; sourced in The Yogi Book (1997)
candidates.whyNotable: One of Berra's genuinely-sourced lines (said about the 1973 pennant race and printed in The Yogi Book), giving the hub a verified anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Failure is an event, not a person.
candidates.trueOrigin: Zig Ziglar, 'See You at the Top' (full form: 'Failure is an event, it is not a person — yesterday ended last night').
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Ziglar line sourced by Wikiquote to 'See You at the Top' — verified anchor content for the hub.

candidates.quote: You can have everything in life you want, if you will just help enough other people get what they want.
candidates.trueOrigin: Zig Ziglar, 'Secrets of Closing the Sale' (1984), a staple of his talks since 'See You at the Top.'
candidates.whyNotable: Ziglar's signature line, sourced by Wikiquote to 'Secrets of Closing the Sale' (1984) — a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Houston, we've had a problem
candidates.whyNotable: Apollo 13 film says 'Houston, we have a problem'; the real 1970 transmission was past tense: 'Houston, we've had a problem.'

candidates.quote: Life moves pretty fast
candidates.whyNotable: Ferris Bueller's Day Off (1986) — often truncated from 'Life moves pretty fast. If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.'

candidates.quote: Me Tarzan, you Jane
candidates.whyNotable: Never said in the Tarzan films; a paraphrase Johnny Weissmuller himself popularized in an interview.

candidates.quote: Mirror, mirror on the wall
candidates.whyNotable: Snow White (1937) — the film says 'Magic mirror on the wall.'

candidates.quote: Well, nobody's perfect
candidates.whyNotable: Some Like It Hot (1959) — genuine closing line; frequently attributed with the wrong speaker/film.

candidates.quote: You're gonna need a bigger boat
candidates.whyNotable: Jaws (1975) — widely misquoted as 'We're gonna need a bigger boat.'

candidates.quote: 640K ought to be enough for anybody
candidates.whyNotable: The internet's favorite Gates quote; he has repeatedly and flatly denied ever saying it.

candidates.quote: Everything that can be invented has been invented
candidates.whyNotable: Attributed to the 1899 US Patent Commissioner; a documented fabrication — he never said it.
