candidates.whyNotable: Frequently circulated as a Disney line, but Wikiquote traces it to Interior Secretary Walter J. Hickel speaking about wolf killing, not Disney.

candidates.quote: Every society honors its live conformists, and its dead troublemakers.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mignon McLaughlin, who published the exact line in her 1963 book The Neurotic's Notebook. Dyer used a version in a 1999 book; the saying is also widely misattributed to Marshall McLuhan (name confusion with McLaughlin).
candidates.whyNotable: Widely credited to Wayne Dyer (and to Marshall McLuhan) but documented by QI to writer Mignon McLaughlin's 1963 The Neurotic's Notebook.

candidates.quote: Before you speak, listen. Before you write, think. Before you spend, earn. Before you invest, investigate. Before you criticize, wait. Before you pray, forgive. Before you quit, try. Before you retire, save. Before you die, give.
candidates.trueOrigin: William Arthur Ward, Thoughts of a Christian Optimist (1968); reassigned to Shakespeare by 2010.
candidates.whyNotable: This 'Before you...' list is widely reshared as Shakespeare, but QI shows it was assembled by inspirational writer William Arthur Ward in 1968.

candidates.quote: The meaning of life is to find your gift. The purpose of life is to give it away.
candidates.trueOrigin: David S. Viscott, Finding Your Strength in Difficult Times (1993).
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared inspirational 'Shakespeare' lines on social media, but it comes from a 1990s self-help book, not the Bard.

candidates.quote: There has never been a statue erected to honor a critic.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jean Sibelius, quoted in Bengt de Törne's 1937 book 'Sibelius: A Close-Up'; Ziglar merely helped repopularize it decades later.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely pinned on Ziglar by 2004, but QI traces it to Finnish composer Jean Sibelius, recorded in a 1937 book saying 'a statue has never been set up in honour of a critic.'

candidates.quote: A penny saved is a penny earned
candidates.trueOrigin: A reworded popular paraphrase; Franklin's genuine 1737 Poor Richard's line was 'A penny saved is two pence clear,' and the 'penny saved is a penny got' form predates Franklin.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted 'Franklin' thrift maxim, but it is a modern paraphrase; his actual Poor Richard's wording was 'A penny saved is two pence clear' (and the earlier 'A penny sav'd is a penny got' predates him).

candidates.quote: The horse is here to stay, but the automobile is only a novelty — a fad.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to the president of the Michigan Savings Bank advising Ford's lawyer Horace Rackham against investing in Ford (c.1903), per Bushnell's 1922 biography.
candidates.whyNotable: Often retold as a prediction about (or even by) Ford's world; QI shows it was a warning made by a banker to Ford's lawyer circa 1903, documented in Sarah Bushnell's 1922 Ford biography — not a Ford quote.

candidates.quote: Knowing is not enough; we must apply. Being willing is not enough; we must do.
candidates.trueOrigin: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 'Wilhelm Meisters Wanderjahre' (German original).
candidates.whyNotable: Widely circulated as a Leonardo motivational line; Wikiquote notes no attribution to him predates its origin in Goethe's 'Wilhelm Meisters Wanderjahre'.

candidates.quote: Live as if you were to die tomorrow. Learn as if you were to live forever.
candidates.trueOrigin: Ancient/medieval aphorism (echoes the Hitopadesha and is attributed to Isidore of Seville, c. 560-636, in the FPA Book of Quotations, 1952, among others); no Gandhi source.
candidates.whyNotable: A graduation-card favorite credited to Gandhi, but Wikiquote documents the aphorism circulating for centuries — attributed variously to Isidore of Seville, Edmund Rich, Alain de Lille and Erasmus — long before Gandhi.

candidates.quote: The greatness of a nation and its moral progress can be judged by the way its animals are treated.
candidates.trueOrigin: David Strauss, The Old Faith and the New (Der alte und der neue Glaube, 1872): 'The manner in which a nation in the aggregate treats animals, is one chief measure of its real civilization.' Attributed to Gandhi since at least 1980.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitous in animal-welfare and vegetarian circles, but Wikiquote finds it in none of Gandhi's Complete Works; the original is by German theologian David Strauss (1872).

candidates.quote: All of us are creatures of a day; the rememberer and the remembered alike.
candidates.trueOrigin: The individual line is genuine (Meditations Book 4.35), but the popular flowing 'quotation' was stitched together from Book 4.35, 7.21, and 12.21 by later editors/translators (associated with Irvin Yalom's 'Creatures of a Day').
candidates.whyNotable: Popularized as a single Marcus Aurelius passage (notably via Irvin Yalom's book title); QI shows the widely circulated version is a composite assembled from three separate Meditations passages rather than one original sentence.

candidates.quote: Marconi is a good fellow. Let him continue. He is using seventeen of my patents.
candidates.trueOrigin: Plausibly a genuine c.1901 Tesla remark but attested only in secondary sources.
candidates.whyNotable: The quintessential Tesla-vs-Marconi radio-priority zinger; Wikiquote files it under Attributed, sourced only to later secondary works (PBS, a 1999 biography) rather than a contemporary record.

candidates.quote: What you do speaks so loudly that I cannot hear what you say.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase of Ralph Waldo Emerson, 'Social Aims' in Letters and Social Aims (1875)
candidates.whyNotable: Genuinely rooted in Emerson but not in this form; QI shows the popular one-liner is an abridged, simplified rewrite of what Emerson actually wrote in 'Social Aims.'

candidates.quote: Trust, but verify.
candidates.trueOrigin: A signature phrase Reagan genuinely used dozens of times, but it originates as a translation of the Russian proverb 'doveryai, no proveryai' — he popularized it, he did not coin it.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Reagan's most-quoted lines that he really did say, but Wikiquote flags that he was quoting an old Russian proverb, not authoring it.

candidates.quote: With all this manure, there must be a pony somewhere!
candidates.trueOrigin: QI documents the joke back to 1902 (an Illinois state senator's banquet tale) with many evolving punchlines; Reagan famously retold it, but it is a century-old anonymous joke he did not originate.
candidates.whyNotable: Reagan's trademark optimism joke, but Quote Investigator traces the 'pony' punchline to a 1902 banquet story long predating him.

candidates.quote: If a man does not know to what port he is steering, no wind is favourable to him.
candidates.trueOrigin: This negative formulation is genuinely Seneca (Epistulae Morales, 'Ignoranti quem portum petat, nullus suus ventus est'). The popular POSITIVE reworded variants ('You must know which harbor you're headed for to catch the right wind') are later paraphrases whose exact wording is not Seneca's; QI documents the centuries-long transformation. Sometimes even misattributed to Oscar Wilde.
candidates.whyNotable: The genuine Seneca aphorism vs. its ubiquitous reworded/positive paraphrase; QI untangles the real Latin line from the modern distortions.

candidates.quote: Contentment is natural wealth, luxury is artificial poverty.
candidates.trueOrigin: Source unknown; appears in Charles Simmons' A Laconic Manual (1852) without attribution
candidates.whyNotable: Circulated as a Socrates aphorism but Wikiquote lists it under Attributed with no original source — it appears in Charles Simmons' 1852 manual with no classical citation.

candidates.quote: I know that I know nothing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase/back-translation of Plato's Apology 21d and Republic 354b-c
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive 'Socratic paradox' — hugely famous but Wikiquote flags the pithy wording as a modern back-translation; it derives loosely from Plato's Apology 21d rather than being a literal quotation.

candidates.quote: We will make electricity so cheap that only the rich will burn candles.
candidates.trueOrigin: Reworded from Edison's 1880 New York Herald remark; modern 'rich' phrasing appeared around 2008.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple energy-optimism quote; QI shows Edison expressed the idea in 1880 but used 'none but the extravagant will burn tallow candles' - the punchy 'only the rich' wording is a much later reformulation.

candidates.quote: I am always doing what I can't do yet in order to learn how to do it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Van Gogh — an 1885 letter to Anthon van Rappard ("ik maak steeds wat ik nog niet kan om het te leeren kunnen"); the rival Picasso attribution is undocumented and post-dates his 1973 death
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently credited to Picasso, but QI confirms it is authentically Van Gogh from an 1885 letter, making it a documented attribution tug-of-war.

candidates.quote: History is but a fable agreed upon
candidates.trueOrigin: Voltaire, Jeannot et Colin (1764), spoken by a character crediting an unnamed wit
candidates.whyNotable: Genuinely traceable to Voltaire's 1764 tale Jeannot et Colin, but QI notes he put the line in a character's mouth crediting an unnamed wit, so the direct attribution is imprecise.

candidates.quote: I will send a barrel of this wonderful whiskey to every general in the army.
candidates.trueOrigin: An anecdote about Grant's drinking printed anonymously in 1863 newspapers; QI notes it mirrors an older King George II / General Wolfe story and that aide Thomas Eckert said Lincoln denied it. Evidence is inconclusive.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous Civil War Lincoln witticism that QI concludes cannot be solidly confirmed or refuted, likely templated on an 18th-century royal anecdote.

candidates.quote: You can fool all the people some of the time, and some of the people all the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time.
candidates.trueOrigin: No contemporaneous record exists; earliest attribution to Lincoln is an 1885 letter by prohibitionist H. Clay Bascom, two decades after Lincoln's death. Also credited to P. T. Barnum.
candidates.whyNotable: Perhaps the single most-quoted 'Lincoln' aphorism, yet QI finds no evidence he ever said it and the phrase only appears in the 1880s.

candidates.quote: Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase via Roger Sessions (NYT, 1950) and Louis Zukofsky (Poetry, 1950); loosely based on Einstein's 1933 Oxford lecture.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitously quoted as Einstein but QI shows the pithy wording is a paraphrase: composer Roger Sessions attributed an 'in effect' version to Einstein in a 1950 New York Times piece, popularized by poet Louis Zukofsky the same year; Einstein's genuine 1933 Oxford lecture expressed the idea far more verbosely.

candidates.quote: Two things are infinite: the universe and human stupidity; and I'm not sure about the universe
candidates.trueOrigin: Frederick (Fritz) Perls, 'Ego, Hunger, and Aggression' (1947); Einstein credit added by Perls in 1969, unverifiable.
candidates.whyNotable: A clever line constantly pinned on Einstein; QI shows it rests entirely on Gestalt therapist Fritz Perls, who first published a version in 1947 crediting 'a great astronomer' and only named Einstein in 1969, with the wording mutating across his books.

candidates.quote: Happiness depends upon ourselves.
candidates.trueOrigin: Translator's gloss by J. A. K. Thomson, The Ethics of Aristotle (1955); not in the original Greek
candidates.whyNotable: Circulates as a tidy Aristotle aphorism; Wikiquote notes it is an interpretive gloss added by translator J. A. K. Thomson (1955) and does not appear in the original Greek at 1099b.29.

candidates.quote: It is the mark of an educated mind to be able to entertain a thought without accepting it.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Aristotelian source; unattributed modern paraphrase
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous 'critical thinking' meme credited to Aristotle; Wikiquote lists it as disputed with no genuine source, possibly a garbling of Nicomachean Ethics 1094b.24.

candidates.quote: Don't cry because it's over. Smile because it happened.
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Seuss (d. 1991) ever said it; assigned to him by 2002. Also credited over the years to Ludwig Jacobowski (1899) and Gabriel Garcia Marquez; QI finds no solid attribution.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Seuss lines; Quote Investigator finds no substantive link to Seuss and traces the Seuss credit only to about 2002.
candidates.notes: Auto-deduped 2026-07-20: already present in corpus as dont-cry-because-its-over-smile-because-it-happened

candidates.quote: All things are subject to interpretation; whichever interpretation prevails at a given time is a function of power and not the truth.
candidates.trueOrigin: Loosely paraphrases a note from Nietzsche's 1888 Nachlass, but the specific 'function of power' wording is not his; commonly circulated without citation.
candidates.whyNotable: Very widely quoted as Nietzsche, but Wikiquote notes it is usually cited without a source and the closest real passage does not mention 'power'.

candidates.quote: When we are tired, we are attacked by ideas we conquered long ago.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attribution to Nietzsche unverified; QI located no supporting citation in his works.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely attributed to Nietzsche, but QI is skeptical — no solid citation to a specific work has been found.

candidates.quote: If people cannot write well, they cannot think well, and if they cannot think well, others will do their thinking for them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not found in Orwell's published works. Attributed to Orwell by John H. Bunzel in Phyllis Schlafly's The Power of the Positive Woman (1977); likely a paraphrase of the Newspeak ideas in 1984.
candidates.whyNotable: A writing-instruction favorite pinned on Orwell that traces only to a 1977 attribution, not his own prose.

candidates.quote: In a time of universal deceit, telling the truth is a revolutionary act.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source in Orwell's works. Earliest published appearance is 1982 (Science Dimension); thematically similar lines predate it (von Raumer 1855, Jean Jaures 1898). QI suggests it began as a summary of Orwell's ideas that was later converted into a direct quote; a 1982 Australian book is the earliest known Orwell attribution.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous protest-poster 'Orwell' quote that appears nowhere in his writing; QI and Wikiquote both find no Orwell source.

candidates.quote: Within any important issue, there are always aspects no one wishes to discuss.
candidates.trueOrigin: No verification in Orwell's writings. It appears in Michael Crichton's novel State of Fear (2004) and Sheila Suess Kennedy's Picking Fights with Thunderstorms (2005), but no Orwell source has been found.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulates as an Orwell aphorism but surfaces only in 2000s books with no trace in his actual work.

candidates.quote: You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with
candidates.trueOrigin: No single author; QI says the saying evolved over time. Earliest related framing appears in a 1989 Parade Magazine article by Daniel G. Amen; the Rohn attribution traces only to Jack Canfield's 2005 book The Success Principles (via Tim Ferriss). QI tentatively lists Rohn as leading candidate but calls the evidence weak.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-shared quote pinned on Jim Rohn; Quote Investigator rates the Rohn attribution as weak, tracing the concept's evolution back to a 1989 Parade article by Daniel Amen and the Rohn credit only to a 2005 Jack Canfield book.

candidates.quote: I like your Christ. I do not like your Christians. Your Christians are so unlike your Christ.
candidates.trueOrigin: No Gandhi source located; nearest documented antecedent is Bara Dada in E. Stanley Jones, The Christ of the Indian Road (1925): 'Jesus is ideal and wonderful, but you Christians -- you are not like him.'
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly quoted in sermons and Christian apologetics, but Wikiquote finds no source in Gandhi's works; a very similar line is attributed to 'Bara Dada' in E. Stanley Jones's The Christ of the Indian Road (1925).

candidates.quote: I think it would be a good idea.
candidates.trueOrigin: Apocryphal; earliest located attribution is a 1967 CBS News documentary 'The Italians' (per Reader's Digest 1967), popularized via E. F. Schumacher's Good Work (1979).
candidates.whyNotable: The famous quip supposedly given when Gandhi was asked what he thought of Western civilization; QI shows the earliest source is a 1967 CBS documentary nearly 20 years after his death, with no film or biographical record of him saying it.

candidates.quote: What is history but a fable agreed upon?
candidates.trueOrigin: Popularized by Napoleon but he disclaimed coinage; QI traces the idea to Voltaire, Fontenelle, or Helvetius.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely quoted as Napoleon's cynicism about history; QI shows he popularized but disclaimed it, with roots in Voltaire, Fontenelle and Helvetius.

candidates.quote: I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine sentiment recorded as 'I have gotten a lot of results! I know several thousand things that won't work' in Edison: His Life and Inventions (1910); modern round-number wording is unsourced.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared motivational Edison lines; QI finds Edison did make a remark of this type (per a 1910 Mallory biography) but this exact 10,000-ways wording is a later polish, not his documented words.

candidates.quote: Doctors are men who prescribe medicines of which they know little, to cure diseases of which they know less, in human beings of whom they know nothing
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Voltaire source; earliest appearances circa 1956
candidates.whyNotable: A much-shared cynical medical quip; Wikiquote notes it only surfaces in publications from 1956 onward with no original French source ever located in Voltaire.

candidates.quote: Etymology is a science in which the vowels count for nothing, and the consonants for very little
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Voltaire source; earliest link is A. W. von Schlegel's 1815 review
candidates.whyNotable: A witty line about linguistics attributed to Voltaire since an 1815 Schlegel review, but neither Wikiquote nor QI can find it anywhere in Voltaire's own writings.

candidates.quote: Men occasionally stumble over the truth, but most of them pick themselves up and hurry off as if nothing had happened
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; earliest evidence Reader's Digest (April 1942), authorship unclear (QI).
candidates.whyNotable: Widely credited to Churchill, but Quote Investigator finds the earliest 1942 Reader's Digest instance and notes the barb was reportedly aimed at Churchill's rival Stanley Baldwin, not spoken by him.

candidates.quote: Never let a good crisis go to waste
candidates.trueOrigin: Popularized by Rahm Emanuel (2008); concept from Saul Alinsky's Rules for Radicals (1971). Not Churchill.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently pinned on Churchill but popularized by Rahm Emanuel in 2008 and rooted in Saul Alinsky's 1971 Rules for Radicals, with no Churchill source.

candidates.quote: This is the sort of bloody nonsense up with which I will not put
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous anecdote; earliest 1942 Strand Magazine version credits an unnamed English master, not Churchill (QI).
candidates.whyNotable: The famous 'don't end a sentence with a preposition' riposte; Quote Investigator finds the earliest 1942 version had no Churchill attribution and involved an anonymous schoolteacher.

candidates.quote: As God is my witness, I'll never go hungry again!
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "As God is my witness, I'll never be hungry again!" — "be hungry," not "go hungry." Spoken by Scarlett O'Hara (Vivien Leigh) as the closing sentence of her first-act curtain speech; Wikiquote transcribes the full speech: "As God is my witness, as God is my witness they're not goin' to lick me. I'm goin' to live through this and when it's all over, I'll never be hungry again. No, nor any of my folk. If I have to lie, steal, cheat or kill. As God is my witness, I'll never be hungry again!" Gone with the Wind (1939), Selznick International Pictures, dist. MGM. Screen credit Sidney Howard, but the writing credit is shared/disputed (see note on uncredited writers).
candidates.whyNotable: AFI #59. The popular rendering swaps "be hungry" for "go hungry" — a single-word drift from the right source, the classic film-misquote shape. The actual wording is solidly transcription-sourced (it appears twice in the Wikiquote transcript), which is exactly the bar a misquote page needs.

candidates.quote: Beam me up, Scotty.
candidates.trueOrigin: Never spoken in Star Trek: The Original Series (Desilu Productions for NBC, 1966-69). Wikiquote records the closest actual line as "Scotty... beam us up" in "The Gamesters of Triskelion" (aired 5 January 1968, written by Margaret Armen). Other genuine in-series variants: "Beam me aboard", "Beam us up home", "Two to beam up". The exact phrase was later spoken in Star Trek: The Animated Series; Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home (1986) has the near-miss "Scotty, beam me up." Rights holder is the studio (Paramount/CBS) under work-for-hire, not the writers.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most famous line Star Trek never contained, and probably the highest-search misquote in the franchise. Wikiquote documents both the non-existence of the popular wording and the closest real line, with an episode — exactly the both-sides-citable case this site exists for. James Doohan (Scotty) titled his 1996 autobiography with the misquote, which shows how completely the wrong version displaced the real ones.

candidates.quote: Damn it, Jim! I'm a doctor, not a...
candidates.trueOrigin: The "I'm a doctor, not a ___" formula is genuine and recurring, but "Damn it" never aired in the original series — Wikiquote notes the closest McCoy or anyone came was the euphemisms "Blast it!" and "Blast!", no profanity beyond "hell" airing in the original run. Actual first instance: "I'm a doctor, not a bricklayer!" — "The Devil in the Dark" (aired 9 March 1967), written by Gene L. Coon. Wikiquote's Misquotations page credits Dan Aykroyd's SNL impersonation with popularising the "Damn it" version; McCoy does say "Damn it, Jim" later, in the film Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan (1982). Studio: Desilu/Paramount for NBC.
candidates.whyNotable: A precise, well-documented drift: the sentence frame is real, one word was bolted on by a parody and then back-propagated onto the source. Wikiquote names both the actual wording and a specific vector for the corruption (SNL), plus the later film that retroactively made the misquote half-true. Heavily searched.

candidates.quote: Do you feel lucky, punk?
candidates.trueOrigin: MISQUOTE — right film, wrong words. Actual line, climax/cliff-scene delivery as transcribed at Wikiquote: "I know what you're thinking, punk. You're thinking 'Did he fire six shots or only five?' Now, to tell you the truth, I've forgotten myself in all this excitement. But being this is a .44 Magnum, the most powerful handgun in the world and it will blow your head clean off, you've gotta ask yourself a question: 'Do I feel lucky? Well, do ya, punk?'" Spoken by Inspector Harry Callahan, played by Clint Eastwood. Dirty Harry (1971), Warner Bros. / The Malpaso Company, directed by Don Siegel. WRITING CREDIT IS SHARED AND THE SPEECH ITSELF IS UNSETTLED: screenplay credited to Harry Julian Fink, R.M. Fink and Dean Riesner (story by Harry Julian Fink & R.M. Fink), with uncredited contributions from John Milius, Terrence Malick and Jo Heims. Milius has claimed the film's guns-and-attitude material; no source consulted assigns this specific speech to one writer, so it should not be attributed to one. ORIGINATION: the line originates in this film — Dirty Harry is an original screenplay (working title "Dead Right"), not adapted from a novel or play; the Philip Rock novelization followed the film. Rights holder is the studio (Warner Bros.), not the screenwriters — screen writing is work-for-hire. NOTE: the speech is delivered twice with different wording, and Wikiquote itself renders the tag as both "do ya, punk?" and "do you, punk?" — see notes.
candidates.whyNotable: The signature wrong-words-from-the-right-source error of American screen quotation, and the single highest-value item for this title: Wikiquote's Misattributed section names it explicitly and gives the real wording, so both halves of the claim are citable from a transcription. The drift is meaningful, not cosmetic — the real line has Harry telling the punk what question the PUNK must ask himself ("Do I feel lucky?", spoken in the punk's voice), which the popular five-word version inverts into Harry taunting him ("Do you feel lucky") and strips of the ~60-word build-up that makes it work. The bolded portion is AFI #51. This is what people search for.

candidates.quote: Fly, my pretties, fly!
candidates.trueOrigin: Never spoken in the film in this or any form: the phrase "Fly, my pretties" does not appear anywhere in the Wikiquote transcription of the 1939 film. The Wicked Witch of the West (Margaret Hamilton) dispatches the winged monkeys with a line containing "Now, fly!" — with no "pretties" in it. The popular version fuses that scene with a DIFFERENT, real line from a different scene, "I'll get you, my pretty, and your little dog too!", in which "my pretty" is SINGULAR and is addressed to Dorothy, not to the monkeys. Screenplay by Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson and Edgar Allan Woolf, The Wizard of Oz (1939), Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (rights holder).
candidates.whyNotable: A pure phantom line of the "Play it again, Sam" class — universally quoted, endlessly parodied, and never said. Unusually well-evidenced for a negative claim: Wikiquote's transcript lacks the phrase entirely, and AFI's independent rendering of the real line (#99) confirms the singular "my pretty" addressed to Dorothy, which is exactly what the misquote pluralises and redirects at the monkeys. The mechanism of the error — two scenes welded together — is itself the story the page should tell.

candidates.quote: Frankly, Scarlett, I don't give a damn.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn." — spoken by Rhett Butler (Clark Gable) to Scarlett O'Hara as the film's closing line. Gone with the Wind (1939), Selznick International Pictures, distributed by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer; rights now with Warner Bros. ORIGINATION: the line is not original to the film — it comes from Margaret Mitchell's 1936 novel, where Rhett says "My dear, I don't give a damn"; the film added the word "Frankly." AUTHORSHIP: sole screen credit went to Sidney Howard (posthumous Best Adapted Screenplay Oscar), but the writing credit is genuinely disputed — Ben Hecht, David O. Selznick, Jo Swerling, Oliver H. P. Garrett, Barbara Keon and John Van Druten all worked on the script uncredited, and Selznick claimed in a memo that most of the dialogue was his own. No source establishes who added "Frankly."
candidates.whyNotable: AFI's #1 movie quotation of all time, and one of the most-misquoted lines in cinema — the public routinely substitutes the character's name ("Scarlett") for "my dear." The Hollywood Reporter includes it on its list of the most famously misquoted films. Highest search demand of anything on this title.

candidates.quote: Go ahead, make my day
candidates.trueOrigin: WRONG WORK, not wrong words — the wording is accurate, but the line is NOT in Dirty Harry (1971) and Harry Callahan never says it there. Wikiquote's Dirty Harry page lists it under Misattributed: "The line 'Go ahead, make my day' isn't uttered by Harry at any point in the film. He instead first uttered it in 1983's Sudden Impact." Sudden Impact is the fourth Dirty Harry film — twelve years and three sequels later. Spoken by Inspector Harry Callahan, played by Clint Eastwood, in the diner-robbery scene; he says a variant ("Come on, make my day") again later. Sudden Impact (1983), Warner Bros. / The Malpaso Company, directed by Clint Eastwood; screenplay by Joseph Stinson, story by Earl E. Smith and Charles B. Pierce. AUTHORSHIP OF THIS LINE IS DISPUTED and should not be assigned to one person: variously credited to John Milius (uncredited contributor), Charles B. Pierce (story) and Joseph Stinson (screenplay). ORIGINATION — the film did not coin the phrase: the confrontational form appears a year earlier in Vice Squad (1982), where a detective says "Come on scumbag, make your move... and make my day!", and "you made my day" as an ordinary pleasantry long predates both. Sudden Impact sharpened and popularised it. (The Vice Squad precedent is sourced to Wikipedia/phrases.org.uk, not to Wikiquote or QI — attribute it accordingly.) Rights holder is Warner Bros., not the writers.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-quoted lines in American film — AFI #6, and a phrase that entered political speech — and the public files it under the wrong movie. Wikiquote documents the error directly on the Dirty Harry page, which is what makes it citable rather than folklore. Doubly corrective: it fixes both the work (Sudden Impact 1983, not Dirty Harry 1971) and the common assumption that the film invented the phrase, when a 1982 film used the confrontational form first. A film credited with a line it borrowed and a film credited with a line from its own sequel are the same error class.

candidates.quote: Greed is good.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "The point is, ladies and gentlemen, that greed, for lack of a better word, is good." — spoken by Gordon Gekko (Michael Douglas), written by Stanley Weiser and Oliver Stone, Wall Street (1987), 20th Century Fox (work-for-hire; studio holds rights). Gekko never says the bare sentence "Greed is good" — he continues "Greed is right, greed works." The AFI ranked the full clause, not the compression, at #57 on 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes. On origination: Oliver Stone's own commentary, quoted on the Wikiquote page, credits the idea to Ivan Boesky's speech saying "Greed is right"; Boesky's own documented remark (Wikiquote, sourced to Den of Thieves, 1992) is "Greed is all right, by the way. I think greed is healthy." — so the film sharpened a real financier's line rather than inventing the sentiment.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line in American finance culture, and the popular form is a compression that is never spoken on screen. Both Wikiquote and the AFI transcribe the longer clause, so the wording claim rests on transcription rather than memory. The Boesky origination is documented on Wikiquote itself via Stone's commentary.

candidates.quote: Hello, Clarice.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "Good evening, Clarice." — screenplay by Ted Tally, from The Silence of the Lambs (1991), dir. Jonathan Demme, Orion Pictures (rights holder; screen writing is work-for-hire). Wikiquote's transcription contains "Good evening, Clarice" and does not contain "Hello, Clarice" anywhere. Lecter never says "Hello, Clarice" at any point in the 1991 film. Origination note: the greeting is the film's own — it is not carried over from Thomas Harris's 1988 novel. The misquote was reinforced by parody, most influentially Jim Carrey's Lecter impression in The Cable Guy (1996), and was later absorbed into the franchise itself when Hopkins does say "Hello, Clarice" in the sequel Hannibal (2001) — which is very likely why the memory feels authentic.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-searched line associated with the film and a textbook Mandela effect: near-universally quoted, never spoken in the movie it is attributed to. Highest-value candidate here — popular wording and transcript demonstrably differ, and both can be cited. The sequel later making it canon is the twist that makes the page worth reading rather than merely correct.

candidates.quote: If that plane leaves the ground and you're not on it, you'll regret it. Maybe not today, maybe not tomorrow, but soon and for the rest of your life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "If that plane leaves the ground and you're not with him, you'll regret it. Maybe not today, maybe not tomorrow, but soon and for the rest of your life." — Rick says "with him" (meaning Victor Laszlo), not "on it". Written by Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein and Howard Koch — Casablanca (1942), dir. Michael Curtiz, Warner Bros. (work-for-hire; rights holder Warner Bros.). Adapted from the unproduced 1940 play "Everybody Comes to Rick's" by Murray Burnett and Joan Alison; whether this line originated in the play is not established by Wikiquote.
candidates.whyNotable: The actual wording is firmly transcribed on Wikiquote's Casablanca page ("not with him"). The drift to "not on it" is transcribed on Wikiquote's own page for Play It Again, Sam (1972), where Allan Felix recites the "not on it" version and then says "It's from Casablanca. I've waited my whole life to say it." — a dated on-screen instance of the misquote inside a film that is itself an homage to Casablanca. CAVEAT FOR EDITORS: Wikiquote does NOT label "not on it" a misquote; that half of the claim is inference from the 1972 transcript, not documentation of popular usage. Do not publish a "commonly misquoted as" assertion on this evidence without a stronger source. Substantively the swap matters — "with him" is the whole point of Rick's argument (she belongs with Victor), which "on it" erases.

candidates.quote: If you build it, they will come.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "If you build it, he will come" — singular "he", not "they". Wikiquote's Misquotations page documents the "they" form explicitly as an error, and the Field of Dreams transcript carries the line only as "If you build it, he will come" (spoken by The Voice, credited on screen as "Himself"). IMPORTANT ORIGINATION POINT: the line did NOT originate with the film. It is from W. P. Kinsella's novel Shoeless Joe (Houghton Mifflin, Boston, 1982), where narrator Ray Kinsella hears a ballpark announcer's voice say it; Phil Alden Robinson carried it into his screenplay for Field of Dreams (1989), which he also directed. Distributed by Universal Pictures (domestic) / Carolco (international); the screenplay is work-for-hire, so the film rights holder is Universal, while the novel's rights sit with Kinsella's estate. The film popularised the line but a page crediting Field of Dreams as its source would repeat the borrowed-line error. The plural drift is meaning-destroying, not cosmetic: the film's whole reveal turns on "he" being Ray's father, not the ballplayers — Shoeless Joe points at the catcher and says "If you build it — he will come." Wikiquote suggests the "they" form may be cross-contaminated with Wayne's World 2's "If you book them, they will come."
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line from the film and one of the most misquoted lines in English. It became a business/tech mantra in the plural form ("build it and they will come") — meaning invest and customers will follow — which is precisely the meaning the film does not carry. The correct singular form ranks #39 on AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes. High search volume, and the popular wording differs from the transcript with both forms citable.

candidates.quote: If you want a friend, get a dog.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "And if you need a friend, get a dog." — need, not want. Spoken by Gordon Gekko (Michael Douglas), written by Stanley Weiser and Oliver Stone, Wall Street (1987), 20th Century Fox. Wikiquote and Quote Investigator transcribe the line identically, QI giving the fuller context: "You win a few; you lose a few; but you keep on fighting. And if you need a friend, get a dog. It's trench warfare out there, pal." On origination: the film did NOT originate the saying. QI traces an 1841 Byron-attributed form, "nobody need want a friend who can get a dog," and a 1941 version from Frank Fay advising director René Clair: if you want a friend in this town, buy yourself a dog. The Washington/Truman form ("If you want a friend in Washington, get a dog") traces to Samuel Gallu's 1975 play Give 'em Hell Harry, and QI concludes Truman very likely never said it.
candidates.whyNotable: Highest-value candidate on this title: the popular wording differs from the transcript by one load-bearing word (want/need), and the wording is confirmed by two independent transcriptions (Wikiquote and QI). It also fails the origination test twice over — the film borrowed a saying already a century old, and the version most people know is the Truman one, which is itself a misattribution traceable to a 1975 play.

candidates.quote: It puts the lotion on its skin, or else it gets the hose again.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "It rubs the lotion on its skin, or else it gets the hose again." — spoken by Jame "Buffalo Bill" Gumb (Ted Levine); The Silence of the Lambs (1991), screenplay by Ted Tally, Orion Pictures (rights holder). The verb is "rubs", not "puts". ORIGINATION CAVEAT — this line appears NOT to have originated with the film: the phrasing "It rubs the lotion on its skin. It does this whenever it is told." is reported to appear in Thomas Harris's 1988 novel, meaning the film popularised rather than coined it; this novel attribution still needs checking against the novel's text and should not be stated flatly until it is. Whether the "or else it gets the hose again" clause specifically is Harris's or Tally's is not established. The "puts" variant is likely contaminated by Gumb's nearby line "Put the fucking lotion in the basket!"
candidates.whyNotable: Heavily quoted and parodied (Family Guy, South Park, and elsewhere), and the public overwhelmingly says "puts" where the film says "rubs" — a one-word drift people will actively contest, which is exactly the kind of page that earns its keep. Carries a second correction under the first: the line is probably Harris's from the 1988 novel, not the screenwriter's, so crediting it to the movie is its own error.

candidates.quote: Life is like a box of chocolates. You never know what you're gonna get.
candidates.trueOrigin: No one says this wording in the film. Wikiquote transcribes two distinct lines: Forrest Gump (Tom Hanks) narrates "My Momma always said life was like a box of chocolates. You never know what you're gonna get," and Mrs. Gump (Sally Field) says "Life is a box of chocolates, Forrest. You never know what you're gonna get." Forrest uses a past-tense simile ("was like"); his mother uses a present-tense metaphor (no "like"). The popular "is like" matches neither. Written by Eric Roth; Forrest Gump (1994), dir. Robert Zemeckis, Paramount Pictures (rights holder — screen writing is work-for-hire). ORIGINATION: the line is Roth's, not Winston Groom's — it does not appear in Groom's 1986 source novel, which the film only adapts loosely; per Snopes, some post-film editions of the novel carried the movie's wording in promotional front matter, which is a likely vector for the confusion. AFI ranked the line #40 in "100 Years...100 Movie Quotes" (2005), rendering it "Mama always said life was like a box of chocolates. You never know what you're gonna get."
candidates.whyNotable: The flagship film misquote and the single highest-value candidate for this title: the popular wording is spoken by nobody, and the drift is documented from BOTH directions — Wikiquote transcribes the two real lines, and Snopes rates the misquote claim True after checking the whole film. Unusually, the film contains two competing real versions and the public has fused them into a third that was never said. The origination angle is exactly our error class: the film gets credited with a line, but the novel it is based on never had it.

candidates.quote: Luke, I am your father.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "No. I am your father." — Star Wars: Episode V — The Empire Strikes Back (1980), screenplay credited to Leigh Brackett & Lawrence Kasdan, story by George Lucas; directed by Irvin Kershner. Rights holder: Lucasfilm Ltd. (work-for-hire), originally distributed by Twentieth Century-Fox. Spoken by Darth Vader (David Prowse on set, voiced by James Earl Jones). The name "Luke" appears nowhere in the line: Vader's "No." is a rebuttal to Luke's preceding line, and Wikiquote transcribes the exchange as Vader: "No. I am your father." / Luke: "No. No. That's not true! That's impossible!" ORIGINATION NOTE: the father revelation was not in Brackett's first draft (February 1978); Brackett died 18 March 1978 and her dialogue and characterization were removed, though Lucas insisted she retain co-writer credit over Writers Guild objections. The revelation entered in Lucas's own handwritten second draft (April 1978) and was refined by Kasdan — so the two credited screenwriters did not originate the line, and the writing credit here is genuinely contested rather than shared cleanly.
candidates.whyNotable: Routinely called the most famous movie misquote in English, and a standard textbook example of the Mandela effect. The inserted vocative "Luke" survives because the true line is unrecognizable out of context, while the misquote is instantly identifiable as Star Wars. High search volume; the wording claim is documented on both sides (popular AND actual) by Wikiquote's Misquotations page, which is exactly the shape this site exists to correct.

candidates.quote: Millions of people who have never died before will be killed.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "Save her — do as your heart tells you to do — and millions will die who did not die before." — Spock, "The City on the Edge of Forever" (aired 6 April 1967). Wikiquote traces the garbled wording to Kermit Schafer's 1973 collection "All Time Great Bloopers", which printed it as if it were a flubbed line; Wikiquote notes the real line is not an absurdity at all, since the episode turns on time travel and altered history. WRITING CREDIT IS DISPUTED: Harlan Ellison holds the sole aired teleplay credit, but the script was rewritten by Steven W. Carabatsos, Gene L. Coon and D. C. Fontana, with a final rewrite by Gene Roddenberry over Christmas/New Year 1966-67. Ellison submitted his own unfilmed draft for awards and contested the changes for decades, suing CBS in 2009 (settled that October). Studio: Desilu Productions for NBC.
candidates.whyNotable: The best-evidenced drift on this title: Wikiquote gives the actual line, the exact publication that introduced the corruption, and a date (1973). It is also a rare documented case of a misquote manufactured by a bloopers book rather than by public memory — the 'blooper' was the book's own transcription error. Lower search volume than the others, but the provenance chain is unusually complete and the disputed authorship is itself a strong story.

candidates.quote: Mirror, mirror on the wall, who's the fairest of them all?
candidates.trueOrigin: Never spoken in the film. Actual line: "Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?" — spoken by Queen Grimhilde (voiced by Lucille La Verne) to the Slave in the Magic Mirror (voiced by Moroni Olsen). The Queen invokes the mirror twice and BOTH times says "Magic Mirror", never "Mirror, mirror"; the second invocation is "Magic Mirror on the wall, who now is the fairest one of all?" Note also the second drift: the film says "the fairest ONE of all", not "the fairest of THEM all". Written by a shared story credit — Ted Sears, Richard Creedon, Otto Englander, Dick Rickard, Earl Hurd, Merrill De Maris, Dorothy Ann Blank and Webb Smith (no single writer can be assigned this line); supervising director David Hand; Walt Disney Productions, which as the work-for-hire employer is the rights holder. ORIGINATION: the popular wording is not an invention — it is the standard English rendering of the Brothers Grimm's 1812 "Sneewittchen" ("Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand"), which the 1937 film deliberately CHANGED to "Magic Mirror". So the phrase predates the film by 125 years and is public domain in itself; the error is pinning it on the Disney film, where it was never said.
candidates.whyNotable: The single highest-value candidate for this title: the popular wording differs from the transcript and both sides can be cited. It is one of the most-cited 'Mandela effect' quotes in circulation, and the origination twist makes it a better page than the usual misquote — the wording people remember is genuinely real, just from the 1812 Grimm tale rather than the film they attribute it to. Snopes rates the claim TRUE and reaches the same Grimm explanation.

candidates.quote: Pay no attention to the man behind the curtain.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "Pay no attention to that man behind the curtain!" — spoken by the Wizard (Frank Morgan); the popular version drops the demonstrative "that". Screenplay by Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson and Edgar Allan Woolf, The Wizard of Oz (1939), Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (rights holder).
candidates.whyNotable: Heavily searched and now a stock idiom in political and media commentary, almost always in the shortened form. WEAKEST OF THE THREE MISQUOTES AND FLAGGED AS SUCH: the drift is a single dropped word, and unlike the Kansas and "pretties" lines, both forms genuinely circulate — so the claim 'the public gets this wrong' is softer here. The actual wording is solidly transcribed at Wikiquote, so the record is safe; the page framing should be gentle, or the candidate dropped, rather than asserting a confident public error.

candidates.quote: Play it again, Sam.
candidates.trueOrigin: Never spoken in the film in this form. Actual lines: Ilsa says "Play it once, Sam, for old times' sake." and then "Play it, Sam. Play 'As Time Goes By'."; Rick's version is simply "Play it." Written by Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein and Howard Koch — Casablanca (1942), dir. Michael Curtiz, Warner Bros. (work-for-hire; rights holder Warner Bros., not the writers). The film is adapted from the unproduced 1940 play "Everybody Comes to Rick's" by Murray Burnett and Joan Alison; Wikiquote does not establish whether this exchange originated in the play or was written for the screen, so the page must not claim the film originated it. The wrong wording was cemented by the title of Woody Allen's 1972 film Play It Again, Sam (dir. Herbert Ross, written by Allen from his own play) — notably the phrase does not appear in that film's dialogue either, only in its title.
candidates.whyNotable: The best-documented misquote in cinema, and Wikiquote flags it in an explicit ==Misattributed== section: "While the lines 'Play it' and 'Play it, Sam' both appear in the film, the line 'Play it again, Sam' never appears in the film." Two errors are bundled: wrong words, and wrong speaker — "Play it, Sam. Play 'As Time Goes By'" is ILSA's line to the piano player, yet the public pins it on Bogart's Rick. AFI ranked the real line #28 in its 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes and notes it is often misquoted this way.

candidates.quote: She can't take much more of this, Captain!
candidates.trueOrigin: Never spoken by Scotty — or anyone — in Star Trek: The Original Series. Wikiquote records the nearest real lines as Spock's "They can't take much more of this" (of the deflector shields, to Commodore Decker) in "The Doomsday Machine" (aired 20 October 1967, written by Norman Spinrad, developed from his unpublished novelette "The Planet Eater"), and Scotty's "It's becoming critical, Captain. We can't handle it." in "Who Mourns for Adonais?" (aired 22 September 1967, written by Gilbert Ralston and Gene L. Coon). Studio: Desilu Productions for NBC.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most parodied lines in television history, and it was never said. Wikiquote is explicit that the famous line is an invention and supplies two separate near-miss transcriptions with episodes and writers. Note the compounding error: the popular version also reassigns to Scotty a line closest to one Spock actually spoke.

candidates.quote: Tomorrow is another day.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line as transcribed: "After all...tomorrow...is another day!" — spoken by Scarlett O'Hara (Vivien Leigh) as the film's final spoken line; AFI lists it as "After all, tomorrow is another day!" (#31). ORIGINATION: this is the most-borrowed line on the title. It is the closing line of Margaret Mitchell's 1936 novel ("After all, tomorrow is another day"), and the saying itself is a proverb centuries older than either — traced to "Tomorrow is a new day" c. 1520 and appearing in England's Helicon (1600). The film neither coined nor originated it. Gone with the Wind (1939), Selznick International Pictures, dist. MGM; screen credit Sidney Howard, writing shared/disputed.
candidates.whyNotable: Heavily credited to the film as an original coinage when it is a proverb the film inherited via the novel — precisely the borrowed-line error class. The popular short form also drops the "After all" that the transcript carries.

candidates.quote: Toto, I don't think we're in Kansas anymore.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "Toto, I've a feeling we're not in Kansas anymore." — spoken by Dorothy Gale (Judy Garland); screenplay by Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson and Edgar Allan Woolf, The Wizard of Oz (1939), Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (rights holder). ORIGINATION: this line is the film's own invention — no equivalent appears in L. Frank Baum's source novel The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900). AFI ranks the actual wording #4 on "100 Years...100 Movie Quotes".
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-misquoted line in the film and one of the most misquoted in cinema. The popular version rebuilds the sentence twice over: "I don't think" replaces "I've a feeling", and "Toto" often migrates to the end ("I don't think we're in Kansas anymore, Toto"). Variants like "I'm afraid we're not in Kansas anymore" also circulate. Both wordings are citable — Wikiquote's transcription and AFI #23... (AFI #4) give the actual, and the misquote is what people search. Highest-value record in this batch.

candidates.quote: We're gonna need a bigger boat.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actual line: "You're gonna need a bigger boat." — spoken by Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) in Jaws (1975). Wikiquote transcribes it in full context: "'Slow ahead.' I can go slow ahead. Come on down here and chum some of this shit. [the shark suddenly appears] You're gonna need a bigger boat." The popular version swaps the pronoun: We're for You're. ORIGINATION: the line did not come from Peter Benchley's 1974 novel, nor from the credited screenplay (Peter Benchley and Carl Gottlieb, based on Benchley's novel) — it is reportedly an ad-lib by Roy Scheider. Wikipedia's AFI-list entry cites William Baer, 'Classic American Films: Conversations with the Screenwriters' (Greenwood, 2008), pp. 201–202, noting 'Reportedly an ad lib' and 'Commonly misquoted as "We're gonna need a bigger boat."' Carl Gottlieb was in practice the primary screenwriter, rewriting nearly the whole script during the nine-week shoot. Because the line is an ad-lib, no writer can be cleanly named as its author — say so rather than crediting Benchley or Gottlieb for it. Rights holder (work-for-hire): Universal Pictures / Zanuck- Brown Company; distributed by Universal Pictures.
candidates.whyNotable: The single highest-value candidate for this title, and the only Jaws misquote any authority documents. Ranked #35 on AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes — where AFI's own official wording is "You're gonna need a bigger boat." The wrong wording is documented from two independent angles: the Misquotes section of the AFI-list article lists '#35: "We're gonna need a bigger boat"' among entries that 'have become well-known but are incorrect' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFI%27s_100_Years...100_Movie_Quotes#Misquotes), and Wikipedia's List of film misquotes carries a dedicated row — popular 'We're gonna need a bigger boat' vs actual 'You're gonna need a bigger boat', Chief Martin Brody / Roy Scheider / Jaws / 1975 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_film_misquotes), sourced to The Hollywood Reporter's 'From Star Wars to Jaws: 22 Films That Are Famously Misquoted' (June 30, 2017). Both wordings are therefore citable, which is the bar this site sets. The ad-lib origin is a second correctable error: the line is routinely credited to the screenwriters and to the novel, and belongs to neither.

candidates.quote: You're dead, Jim.
candidates.trueOrigin: McCoy never says "You're dead" to Kirk in the series. The genuine recurring line is "He's dead, Jim" (variants "She's..." / "It's..."), always spoken over someone other than Kirk. Wikiquote notes the misquote is typically pinned on moments where Kirk appears to die, particularly "Amok Time" (aired 15 September 1967, written by Theodore Sturgeon) and "The Tholian Web" (aired 15 November 1968). A catchphrase recurring across many episodes, so it carries no single writing credit. Desilu/Paramount for NBC, 1966-69.
candidates.whyNotable: A grammatical-person error rather than a word swap: the real catchphrase exists, but the second-person form addressed to Kirk never occurred, because the joke of the line depends on McCoy pronouncing someone ELSE dead. Wikiquote documents it and names the specific episodes that seeded the confusion. Lower search volume; include only if the queue has room.

candidates.quote: Those who deny freedom to others deserve it not for themselves, and, under a just God, cannot long retain it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Abraham Lincoln
candidates.whyNotable: Lincoln's crisp moral case that freedom denied to some cannot be secured for anyone.

candidates.quote: If A is success in life, then A equals X plus Y plus Z. Work is X, play is Y and Z is keeping your mouth shut
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine Einstein; Samuel J. Woolf interview, New York Times Magazine, August 1929.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely-sourced and widely-shared Einstein line; QI confirms it to a Samuel J. Woolf interview in the New York Times Magazine, August 1929.

candidates.quote: Imagination is more important than knowledge. Knowledge is limited. Imagination encircles the world
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuine Einstein; Viereck interview, Saturday Evening Post, October 26, 1929.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Einstein's most-quoted genuine lines; QI verifies it to George Sylvester Viereck's 1929 Saturday Evening Post interview, reprinted in Einstein's 1931 'Cosmic Religion.'
candidates.notes: Auto-deduped 2026-07-20: already present in corpus as imagination-is-more-important-than-knowledge

candidates.quote: A little learning is a dangerous thing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Alexander Pope
candidates.whyNotable: The proverbial warning against overestimating shallow knowledge — intellectual humility in one line.

candidates.quote: Hope springs eternal in the human breast
candidates.trueOrigin: Alexander Pope
candidates.whyNotable: A proverb-become-idiom; the canonical way to say that people keep hoping no matter what.

candidates.quote: 'Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all.
candidates.trueOrigin: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive proverb about loving despite loss, quoted for over 170 years and correctly traceable to Tennyson (not Shakespeare, as often misattributed).

candidates.quote: For man, when perfected, is the best of animals, but, when separated from law and justice, he is the worst of all.
candidates.trueOrigin: Aristotle
candidates.whyNotable: The foundational Western statement that law and justice are what make humanity civilized rather than the most dangerous of creatures.

candidates.quote: Happiness is an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.
candidates.trueOrigin: Aristotle
candidates.whyNotable: The foundational Western definition of eudaimonia — happiness as a way of living, not a passing feeling.

candidates.quote: Hope is the dream of a waking man
candidates.trueOrigin: Aristotle
candidates.whyNotable: The oldest and most epigrammatic pick — a crisp, classical one-liner that adds ancient-era gravitas.

candidates.quote: Dost thou love life? Then do not squander time, for that's the stuff life is made of.
candidates.trueOrigin: Benjamin Franklin
candidates.whyNotable: Franklin's famous equation of time with the substance of life itself — endlessly quoted in productivity and how-we-spend-our-days contexts.

candidates.quote: Those who would give up essential Liberty, to purchase a little temporary Safety, deserve neither Liberty nor Safety
candidates.trueOrigin: Franklin, in the Pennsylvania Assembly's reply to the Governor, November 11, 1755.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, sourced Franklin line (1755 Pennsylvania Assembly reply) that anchors the hub with a real quote - and is itself constantly misquoted and stripped of context online.

candidates.quote: I have made this longer than usual because I have not had time to make it shorter.
candidates.trueOrigin: Blaise Pascal
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive quote on why simplicity is hard work — genuinely Pascal's, and the true origin of the popular 'shorter letter' line.

candidates.quote: I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
candidates.trueOrigin: Booker T. Washington
candidates.whyNotable: Reframes success around setbacks overcome rather than status reached — a hard-won, lived-experience take on failure and perseverance.

candidates.quote: No race can prosper till it learns that there is as much dignity in tilling a field as in writing a poem.
candidates.trueOrigin: Booker T. Washington
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive statement on the dignity of manual labor, from Washington's own autobiography.

candidates.quote: Reflect upon your present blessings, of which every man has many; not on your past misfortunes, of which all men have some.
candidates.trueOrigin: Charles Dickens
candidates.whyNotable: A warm, plainspoken call to count blessings from one of English literature's most beloved voices.

candidates.quote: A true friend is, as it were, a second self.
candidates.trueOrigin: Cicero
candidates.whyNotable: The foundational classical definition of friendship as another self, echoed by writers from Montaigne to Emerson.

candidates.quote: Fan Ch'ih asked about benevolence. The Master said, 'It is to love all men.'
candidates.trueOrigin: Confucius
candidates.whyNotable: The core Confucian teaching that benevolence (ren) simply means loving all people; adds ancient, cross-cultural range.

candidates.quote: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
candidates.trueOrigin: Confucius
candidates.whyNotable: A canonical Confucian line on education that pairs study and reflection — a natural centerpiece for any talk on learning.

candidates.quote: When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Confucius
candidates.whyNotable: An ancient, primary-source line on the core lesson of failure: recognize the mistake and correct it without fear.

candidates.quote: When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it — this is knowledge.
candidates.trueOrigin: Confucius
candidates.whyNotable: The canonical Eastern formulation of knowing your limits; endlessly used on slides about honest self-assessment.

candidates.quote: How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.
candidates.trueOrigin: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted opening line in the English love-poetry canon, endlessly used on cards, weddings, and slides.

candidates.quote: Hope is the thing with feathers - that perches in the soul
candidates.trueOrigin: Emily Dickinson
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line in English about hope — the metaphor everyone reaches for on slides, cards, and title pages.

candidates.quote: If a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts; but if he will be content to begin with doubts he shall end in certainties.
candidates.trueOrigin: Francis Bacon
candidates.whyNotable: The canonical epigram on how honest doubt, not premature certainty, is the road to real knowledge.

candidates.quote: Knowledge itself is power.
candidates.trueOrigin: Francis Bacon
candidates.whyNotable: The origin of the world's most-quoted maxim on knowledge, popularly shortened to 'Knowledge is power' and endlessly used on slides.

candidates.quote: Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will.
candidates.trueOrigin: Frederick Douglass
candidates.whyNotable: The canonical line on how power is never surrendered voluntarily but must be confronted; a cornerstone of civil-rights rhetoric.

candidates.quote: He who has a why to live can bear almost any how.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Nietzsche — 'Twilight of the Idols' (Gotzen-Dammerung, 1889), 'Maxims and Arrows'.
candidates.whyNotable: A rare case that is both hugely popular and genuine; QI confirms it is Nietzsche and notes Viktor Frankl later popularized it with credit.

candidates.quote: If we have our own why in life, we shall get along with almost any how.
candidates.trueOrigin: Friedrich Nietzsche
candidates.whyNotable: The origin of the 'find your why' idea (later popularized by Viktor Frankl) — meaning as what makes any hardship bearable.

candidates.quote: That which does not kill me makes me stronger.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Nietzsche — 'Twilight of the Idols' (1889), 'Maxims and Arrows' No. 8.
candidates.whyNotable: Nietzsche's single most quoted line and a genuine one — a strong real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: What does not kill me makes me stronger.
candidates.trueOrigin: Friedrich Nietzsche
candidates.whyNotable: The archetypal aphorism on setbacks as strengthening — endlessly quoted on resilience through adversity.

candidates.quote: When you gaze long into an abyss the abyss also gazes into you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Nietzsche — 'Beyond Good and Evil' (1886), Aphorism 146.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely-sourced, endlessly-quoted line; a solid verified anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: I would maintain that thanks are the highest form of thought; and that gratitude is happiness doubled by wonder.
candidates.trueOrigin: G. K. Chesterton
candidates.whyNotable: The famous 'happiness doubled by wonder' line — a staple on slides and in gratitude books, and elegantly quotable.

candidates.quote: For the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs.
candidates.trueOrigin: George Eliot
candidates.whyNotable: The famous closing sentence celebrating the unseen everyday kindnesses that quietly improve the world.

candidates.quote: Optimism is the faith that leads to achievement; nothing can be done without hope
candidates.trueOrigin: Helen Keller
candidates.whyNotable: Directly ties hope to optimism and action, from an author whose life embodies the theme — ideal for motivational contexts.

candidates.quote: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry David Thoreau
candidates.whyNotable: The canonical American statement of living on purpose — the chapter is literally titled 'What I Lived For'.

candidates.quote: If one advances confidently in the direction of his dreams, and endeavors to live the life which he has imagined, he will meet with a success unexpected in common hours.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry David Thoreau
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line on aspiration and self-directed success, and a perennial slide/graduation staple.

candidates.quote: It takes two to speak the truth, — one to speak, and another to hear.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry David Thoreau
candidates.whyNotable: Frames truth as a shared act requiring an honest listener — a fresh, quotable angle beyond the usual proverbs.

candidates.quote: Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity! I say, let your affairs be as two or three, and not a hundred or a thousand.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry David Thoreau
candidates.whyNotable: The single most iconic literary rallying cry for cutting life down to essentials — the canonical simplicity quote on slides and in books.

candidates.quote: This world is but canvas to our imaginations.
candidates.trueOrigin: Henry David Thoreau
candidates.whyNotable: A poetic statement that reality is raw material for the creative mind; confirmed in the primary text (the popular "a canvas" wording is a slight paraphrase).

candidates.quote: You could not step twice into the same river; for other waters are ever flowing on to you.
candidates.trueOrigin: Heraclitus
candidates.whyNotable: The founding image of change in Western thought — flux as the nature of reality, the original 'you can't step in the same river twice.'

candidates.quote: Seize the day, trusting as little as possible in the future.
candidates.trueOrigin: Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus)
candidates.whyNotable: The original 'carpe diem' — arguably the single most famous line ever written about seizing the present moment.

candidates.quote: If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants.
candidates.trueOrigin: Isaac Newton
candidates.whyNotable: The most-quoted line about crediting those who came before you — humility as acknowledging you build on others' work.

candidates.quote: Shall we make a new rule of life from tonight: always to try to be a little kinder than is necessary?
candidates.trueOrigin: J. M. Barrie
candidates.whyNotable: The genuine, sourced origin of the popular 'always be a little kinder than necessary' line.

candidates.quote: Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
candidates.whyNotable: The most-quoted opening line in political philosophy on freedom versus the constraints of society.

candidates.quote: any man's death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind; and therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee
candidates.trueOrigin: John Donne
candidates.whyNotable: The origin of "for whom the bell tolls" — every death is a personal loss, the definitive line on mortality and human interconnection.

candidates.quote: To live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Henry Newman
candidates.whyNotable: Ties personal growth directly to change itself — one of the most-quoted lines equating maturity with willingness to change.

candidates.quote: Ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Stuart Mill
candidates.whyNotable: The canonical statement of the 'paradox of happiness' — that it comes only when not pursued directly.

candidates.quote: The only freedom which deserves the name, is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Stuart Mill
candidates.whyNotable: The classic liberal statement of individual liberty and the right to choose, endlessly cited in law and ethics.

candidates.quote: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
candidates.trueOrigin: King James Bible (Book of Proverbs)
candidates.whyNotable: The canonical scriptural line on loyalty through hardship, endlessly used at weddings, eulogies, and in books on friendship.

candidates.quote: In the highest antiquity, the people did not know that there were their rulers. In the next age they loved them and praised them. In the next they feared them; in the next they despised them. Their work was done and their undertakings were successful, while the people all said, 'We are as we are, of ourselves.'
candidates.trueOrigin: Lao Tzu
candidates.whyNotable: The origin of the classic servant-leadership maxim that the best leader is barely felt, so the people credit themselves — the canonical 'they will say: we did it ourselves' line.

candidates.quote: He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty.
candidates.trueOrigin: Lao Tzu (Laozi)
candidates.whyNotable: The great ancient counterpoint that reframes true power as self-mastery rather than dominion over others; a distinct, non-Western angle.

candidates.quote: As a well-spent day brings happy sleep, so life well used brings happy death.
candidates.trueOrigin: Leonardo da Vinci
candidates.whyNotable: Links a good death to a well-lived life — a graceful legacy line, gentler and more affirming than the Stoic memento mori.

candidates.quote: Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
candidates.trueOrigin: Lord Acton (John Dalberg-Acton)
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted line in the English language about how authority erodes character; the definitive slide quote on power.

candidates.quote: Confine yourself to the present.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marcus Aurelius
candidates.whyNotable: The most compact Stoic statement of the present-moment theme, from the canonical primary text on living now rather than in past or future.

candidates.quote: Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marcus Aurelius
candidates.whyNotable: The core Stoic memento mori — because death is always near, live well now; squarely "living in its light."

candidates.quote: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marcus Aurelius
candidates.whyNotable: Modesty as quiet action over self-display; the public-domain original of the popular 'Be one' rendering.

candidates.quote: Observe always that everything is the result of a change, and get used to thinking that there is nothing Nature loves so well as to change existing forms and to make new ones like them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marcus Aurelius
candidates.whyNotable: Reframes change as Nature's deepest preference, not disruption — reassuring for talks about transformation and renewal.

candidates.quote: The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marcus Aurelius
candidates.whyNotable: The Stoic core of resilience — obstacles are not blocks but fuel; a slide-ready favorite in leadership and adversity talks.

candidates.quote: Think not so much of what thou hast not as of what thou hast: but of the things which thou hast select the best, and then reflect how eagerly they would have been sought, if thou hadst them not.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marcus Aurelius
candidates.whyNotable: The definitive Stoic prescription for gratitude — appreciate what you have by imagining life without it.

candidates.quote: Very little is needed to make a happy life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marcus Aurelius
candidates.whyNotable: The classic Stoic line on contentment through simplicity; genuinely from Meditations (exact wording varies by translation).

candidates.quote: A grateful mind is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all the other virtues.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marcus Tullius Cicero
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-quoted classical line on gratitude, and it names gratitude as the root of every other virtue.

candidates.quote: Since the dawn of history the negro has owned the continent of Africa, rich beyond the dream of poet's fancy, crunching acres of diamonds beneath his bare black feet.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thomas Dixon Jr.'s 1905 novel 'The Clansman,' where the words are spoken by a character; never written by Darwin.
candidates.whyNotable: A racist passage circulated online as proof of Darwin's bigotry; Wikiquote documents that it is not Darwin at all but lifted from a 1905 novel — a high-value debunk that clears a fabricated attribution.

candidates.quote: How do you feel about Hitler sharing yours?
candidates.trueOrigin: Fabricated exchange with no documented source; Ali never said it. Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed, citing Snopes.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral fabricated 'clapback' where Ali supposedly rebukes a reporter linking Islam to 9/11; flagged as misattributed on Wikiquote and debunked by Snopes.

candidates.quote: The problem with quotes on the internet is you can't verify their authenticity
candidates.whyNotable: A self-referential joke quote — perfect for a fact-check site to own.
candidates.notes: Skipped 2026-07-20: self-referential internet gag, not a sincere misattribution. Nobody credits Lincoln with it in earnest, and there is no origin to trace to a primary source, so there is no correct attribution to restore. Out of scope for a primary-source verification corpus.
